passages.title: The Romans' defeat and coming victory
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat open Sūrat ar-Rūm with a piece of news no one in Makkah could have guessed: a defeated empire on the far side of the desert will win again, within a few years, and when it does the believers will rejoice. What holds the passage together is the sentence in its middle — **"The decision of the matter, before and after, is only with Allah"** (ayah 4). The rise and fall of superpowers is the illustration; Allah's sole command over history is the point; and ayah 7 names the reason most people miss it — they know only the outer shell of this life and are heedless of the Hereafter.

## The world these ayat fell into

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a line back to the closing verse of the preceding sūrah, al-ʿAnkabūt, where Allah promised those who strive in His way that He would open His paths to them and bring them to their objectives. The story that opens Sūrat ar-Rūm, it says, is a manifestation of exactly that divine help — help arriving through events the believers had no hand in at all.

Two empires dominated that world. Persia, whose people were fire-worshippers; and Rome — *ar-Rūm* — who were Christians, and therefore People of the Book. Both were in disbelief. But as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the Romans were relatively closer to the Muslims: many of their beliefs — faith in the Hereafter, in prophethood, in revelation — were shared with Islam. The Prophet ﷺ made use of precisely that common ground when he wrote to the king of Rūm inviting him to Islam with the words *"Come to a word common between us and you"* (3:64). Indeed, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it was this very affinity between Islam and Christianity that provoked the Persians to attack Rome.

So when Persia crushed Rome, the two camps in Makkah reacted in opposite directions. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), in a report recorded by Imam Ahmad, said the idolaters wanted the Persians to prevail because they too were idol worshippers, while the Muslims wanted the Romans to prevail because they were People of the Book. The narration of Niyār ibn Mukram al-Aslamī, recorded by at-Tirmidhī, adds the sharper edge: the Quraysh backed Persia because neither Quraysh nor Persia followed a Book, and neither believed in the Resurrection.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Hātim, records that they rejoiced and taunted the Muslims — your favourites have lost — and pressed the analogy home: as the Persian idolaters beat the Roman Christians, so we Makkans will beat you down. This hurt the Muslims. These ayat came down onto that wound.

## Alif Lām Mīm, and "the nearest land"

The sūrah opens with the disconnected letters, **الٓمٓ**. Ibn Kathīr does not restate their meaning here; he simply refers the reader back to his discussion at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah.

**Ayah 3** locates the defeat *fī adnā al-ard* — "in the nearest land." Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and others identified the place as the stretch between Adhruʿāt and Busrā, on the edge of Ash-Shām along the border with the Hijāz; Hāfiz Ibn Hajar, as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, likewise places the war in Syria between those two towns. Mujāhid described it as a place in the Arabian Peninsula closer to Roman territory than to Persian. The geography is part of the point: the defeat happened not on some unknown frontier but on the near edge of the Arabs' own world.

**Who were the Romans?** Ibn Kathīr traces them to al-ʿĪs ibn Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm — cousins of the Children of Isrāʼīl, also called Banū al-Asfar. They followed the religion of the Greeks, worshipping the seven planets and praying toward the north, until roughly three centuries after the Messiah, when Constantine the son of Costas entered Christianity at the invitation of his mother, who had become Christian before him. Ibn Kathīr records the gathering of three hundred and eighteen bishops who reached an agreement and presented their creed to Constantine — "this is what they call the Great Trust," he writes, "but in fact it is the Worst Betrayal." They changed the religion of the Messiah (peace be upon him), adding some things and taking others away — turning their prayer toward the east, moving the Sabbath rites to Sunday, worshipping the cross, permitting the eating of pigs, and adopting innovated observances, offices and monasticism.

## Abū Bakr's wager

In the report of Ibn ʿAbbās (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī, at-Tirmidhī grading it *Hasan Gharīb*), the matter was mentioned to Abū Bakr, who took it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: **"They will certainly prevail."** Abū Bakr carried that to the idolaters, who demanded a time limit with stakes on both sides. He set five years — and the Romans did not prevail. When he reported this back, the Prophet ﷺ said, *"Why did you not make it less than —"* the narrator thinking he said *ten*. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explained: *bidʿ* means less than ten. Then the Romans were victorious, and the ayat stood confirmed.

Niyār ibn Mukram al-Aslamī's account (at-Tirmidhī, graded *Hasan*) fills in the street-level scene. When the ayat came down, Abū Bakr went out proclaiming them through Makkah. Some of the Quraysh challenged him to a bet — this was before betting was forbidden — and reasoned that since *bidʿ* spans three to nine years, they should agree on the middle: six. Six years passed with no Roman victory, and the idolaters collected their stake. In the seventh year the Romans won. The Muslims rebuked Abū Bakr for having agreed to six years, and he answered simply: *"Because Allah said: 'In bidʿ years.'"* The narration ends with the detail that matters most — **at that time, many people became Muslim.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits a separate and fuller account from Ibn Jarīr, naming the opponent: ʿUbayy ibn Khalaf, who told Abū Bakr it could not be so and that he was lying. Abū Bakr staked ten camels on three years. He then went to the Prophet ﷺ and narrated the episode, and the Prophet ﷺ told him he should not have fixed three years, because the Qurʼān said *bidʿ sinīn* — "a few years" — under which the limit could be anything from three to nine. He instructed him to go back and raise the wager to a hundred camels over nine years (seven, in some reports). ʿUbayy accepted at once. Fearing Abū Bakr might leave Makkah, ʿUbayy demanded a guarantor, and Abū Bakr appointed his son ʿAbd ar-Rahmān. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the episode five years before the hijrah and says that after exactly seven years, at the time of the battle of Badr, the Romans defeated the Persians. ʿUbayy had died by then; Abū Bakr claimed the hundred camels from his heirs, and they handed them over.

**The lesson inside the correction.** These are two distinct narrations, not one wager corrected twice — the sources do not present them as a single continuous episode, and the numbers differ. But a single note sounds through both: the term Abū Bakr had fixed did not match the width of the word revelation actually used. He was not doubting — he was proclaiming this news publicly and staking his property on it. A believer's confidence should sit precisely where the text puts it: certain of *what* is promised, unhurried about *when*, and unshaken when the early years pass with nothing visible happening.

## The camels, and a ruling still in motion

When Abū Bakr won the bet and took possession of the hundred camels, he brought them to the Prophet ﷺ, who told him to give them away in charity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the wording attributed to this — *"this is suht; give it in charity"* — as quoted by Abū Yaʿlā in Ibn ʿAsākir on the authority of al-Barāʼ ibn ʿĀzib, via Rūh ul-Maʿānī.

Gambling (*qimār*) is categorically forbidden by the Qurʼān — Allah calls wine, gambling, altar-stones and divining arrows *"filth, a work of Shaytān"* (5:90) — and betting, where money or goods are staked and won or lost on agreed terms, is a form of it. But that prohibition came after the hijrah to Madīnah, alongside the ban on wine; this wager predates it, so the camels were not unlawful when won. Why then give them away? Because, the jurists answer, the Prophet ﷺ did not like earnings from gambling even at that time, and such gain was below Abū Bakr's stature — just as he ﷺ and Abū Bakr never tasted wine even in the years when it was not yet prohibited.

As for the word *suht*: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes first that the scholars of hadith did not accept that particular narration as correct, and second that even if accepted as authentic, *suht* carries more than one meaning — unlawful, but also abominable and undesirable. It cites Imam Rāghib al-Isfahānī's *Mufradāt al-Qurʼān* and Ibn al-Athīr's *an-Nihāyah* for that range of usage. There is also a legal argument for the milder reading: property that is genuinely unlawful must be returned to the person it was taken from, and may only be given away in charity when the owner is unknown, when delivery to him is impossible, or when some religious complication blocks the return — none of which applied here.

## How the impossible actually happened

Ibn Kathīr tells the reversal as a story. The Persian king — he names him Sābūr Dhū al-Aktāf, while Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubī, speaks of Chosroes Parvez — overran Ash-Shām and the outlying Roman lands until Heraclius had nothing left but Constantinople, besieged there for a long, grinding period. The city held only because it was well fortified and half of it faced the sea, so supplies kept coming.

Then Heraclius devised a clever trick. He asked Chosroes for terms of peace, and Chosroes named a ransom so vast that the two kings' combined wealth would not have covered a tenth of it. Heraclius played along, asking leave to travel out to Ash-Shām and his other regions to gather it from his storehouses. He rode not to his treasuries but straight into Persian territory, until he reached al-Madāʼin, the seat of Chosroes' power, seized its treasures, and sent Chosroes' own son back shaved and humiliated on a donkey with the message: *this is what you asked for, so take it*. Chosroes, enraged, renewed the siege and moved to hold the one river ford by which Heraclius could return. Heraclius sent men roughly a day upstream to throw straw and animal droppings into the water; seeing the debris float past, the Persians assumed the Romans had gone that way and rode off in pursuit, leaving the ford clear. The Romans jumped into the river, crossed, and reached Constantinople. Ibn Kathīr calls it a great day for the Christians, and notes that Persia's own land was left devastated, its wealth seized and its people taken captive.

**Why the prediction was extraordinary.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point sharply: in the world of causes and effects, the prediction that Rome would beat Persia had no basis in the visible possibilities when it was made — the way the Persians had beaten the Roman Empire had left no room for their rising again. ʿUbayy's unshaken confidence was, on the evidence of the time, not misconceived. Maʿārif even quotes the historian Edward Gibbon, who observed that at the time this prediction is said to have been delivered, no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment, since Heraclius' first twelve years announced the approaching dissolution of the empire. Muhammad Taqī ʿUsmānī draws the conclusion: had this not been news given by Allah, nobody could have dared predict so unlikely an event — least of all a claimant to prophethood, who would be putting his whole future at stake. This foretelling is therefore among the solid proofs of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

## "The decision of the matter, before and after"

Ayah 4 pivots from history to its Owner. Persia's victory was by Allah's command; Rome's comeback was by Allah's command — *before and after*. That is the passage's real consolation for the believers whom the Quraysh's taunting had hurt: what looks like the momentum of events is in fact the unfolding of a decision that was never in other hands.

## Whose help, and whose joy?

**Ayat 4–5** say the believers will rejoice *"with the help of Allah"* — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out more than one reading without forcing a choice.

- **Read plainly**, the wording apparently implies that the help is Allah's help *to the people of Rūm*. Though they too were disbelievers, their *kufr* was light compared to others', so their being helped by Allah was not a far-fetched thing — especially when it was a matter of happiness for the Muslims.
- **Or the help is to the Muslims themselves**, in two ways (from Rūh): first, the Muslims had presented the victory of Rome as a sign of the truthfulness of the Qurʼān and of Islam, so Rome's victory was in fact the Muslims' victory — and indeed the narration says many people accepted Islam when it landed. Second, there were two great disbelieving powers at that time, and by making them fight each other Allah weakened them both, which is what helped the Muslims defeat them later.
- **Or both at once**: Ibn ʿAbbās and others report that news of Rome's victory reached the Muslims on the very day they defeated the pagans of Makkah at Badr, so that one delight was added to the other. On that reading the "rejoicing of the believers with Allah's help" refers to the victory at Badr itself, and the glad tiding is twofold — one concerning the Romans, one concerning the believers.

Then ayah 5 lifts the whole thing above the two armies: **"He helps whom He wills, and He is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful."** Victory was never a possession either empire owned; it is given, to whomever He wills — *al-ʿAzīz* and *ar-Rahīm*.

## "A promise from Allah"

**Ayah 6** stamps the whole announcement: *"A promise from Allah, and Allah fails not in His promise, but most men know not."* It sits exactly where a listener's doubt would sit — after a claim that sounded absurd, before the years it would take to come true. The verse does not argue the point; it names the Speaker. And it names the failure of the rest: not that they disbelieved the news, but that they *do not know*.

## They know only the surface

**Ayah 7** diagnoses that ignorance, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it beautifully. These people, it says, were quite conversant with worldly needs — how to trade, which commodity to deal in, where to buy and where to sell; how to till, when to sow, when to harvest; how to construct buildings and furnish them with luxuries. Their failure was not incompetence. It was that they were totally ignorant and negligent of the other aspect of this very worldly life, the aspect that is in fact more important: that a person is not a permanent resident here. His stay is temporary — Maʿārif likens it to a visitor on a tourist visa — his permanent abode is the Hereafter, and the provisions he must collect here for his comfort there are true faith and righteous deeds. That simple and straightforward reality, it says, is what these so-called intellectuals did not understand.

**A grammatical detail worth pausing on.** The word is *zāhiran*, carrying *tanwīn* — the indefinite ending, so "*something* superficial" rather than "*what* is superficial." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: even the superficial things of worldly life are not fully known to them. They grasp one aspect of it, are ignorant of its other aspects, and are wholly negligent of the Hereafter. The verse is not conceding worldly mastery to them; it is shrinking their expertise to the sliver it actually is.

**Living it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this on our own age directly. The Qurʼān is full of admonitory stories of people who made a name for themselves collecting every comfort and luxury and then met a disastrous end in this very world, before the everlasting torment of the next — and no sane person calls that sagacious. Yet today the height of wisdom is attributed to whoever accumulates the most wealth and arranges the best comforts, however low he may be in morals; to call such a person wise, it says, is an insult to wisdom by both religious and moral standards. By the Qurʼān's measure, the wise are those conscious of Allah and the Hereafter, who strive for the comforts of the next life and keep their worldly needs at the level at which such needs are necessary, not making their attainment the sole purpose of living. Maʿārif closes with the portrait of true wisdom in 3:190–191: those who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and ponder on the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying *"Our Lord, You have not created all this in vain. We proclaim Your purity. So, save us from the punishment of Fire."*

That is the arc of these seven ayat: a war the Muslims had no part in, a prediction no strategist would have made, a promise that took years to arrive — and a closing verse explaining why so many people watch such things happen and learn nothing from them.

passages.title: Reflect within yourselves and on ruined nations
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** These three ayat put two witnesses in front of a person who has forgotten the Hereafter: the witness of his own reasoning, and the witness of what happened to earlier nations. Ayah 8 calls him to reflect — this universe was not created in vain, so there must be a reckoning. Ayah 9 sends him out on the road to look at what became of nations far stronger than he is. Ayah 10 delivers the verdict on those nations, and names exactly what destroyed them: they denied the signs of Allah and made a mockery of them.

## What holds the three together

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the first two of these ayat are "an appendix and endorsement" to the subject just before them — that these disbelievers are so engrossed in the temporary glitter of this world and its transitory pleasures that they have totally forgotten the real nature of this world and its ultimate end.

So Allah addresses that forgetfulness twice over, from two different directions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the distinction sharply: ayah 8 is "a matter of logical rationale." Ayah 9 then brings forward "worldly thinking and experiences… as a testimony" — evidence you can walk up to and touch. Reason first, then the record of the past. Ayah 10 is the closing summation of both.

That is why the two are built on the same frame: *a-wa lam yatafakkarū* ("have they not reflected…") and *a-wa lam yasīrū* ("have they not travelled…"). Both come as questions, and the question already carries its answer: the evidence is not hidden, and they simply have not bothered to look.

## Ayah 8: "Have they not reflected upon their own being?"

Ibn Kathir renders the opening phrase, *a-wa lam yatafakkarū fī anfusihim*, as "Do they not reflect upon themselves?", and glosses it as "thinking and pondering how Allah created various things in the upper and lower realms and in the space between."

Ibn Kathir heads this section **"Signs of Tawhid"**, and states its conclusion: pondering His creation will show that He exists, that He is Unique in creating it, and that there is no god nor lord besides Him. The chain runs: look at what has been made → recognise the One who made it → recognise that He alone deserves to be worshipped.

**"Except with truth and for an appointed term."** These are the two hinges of the ayah. Ibn Kathir explains that the reflecting person realises "that this was not created in jest or in vain, but in truth, and that it will continue until an appointed time, the Day of Resurrection."

Notice what those two phrases do together. *With truth* means the universe has a point. *For an appointed term* means it has an end already fixed. A thing with a purpose and a deadline is a thing that will be assessed when the deadline arrives. The Hereafter is not an extra doctrine bolted onto belief in a Creator; it follows from taking the creation seriously.

## Why reflection must arrive at the Hereafter

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the reasoning at length, and it is worth following step by step, because this is the argument the ayah is inviting the reader to reconstruct for himself:

1. There is a great wisdom and purpose behind the creation of the sky, the earth and the creatures in between; the Creator did not create them just for nothing.
2. That purpose is that people should recognise the Creator through all His creations — and then get on to look for the things that He likes and dislikes.
3. Once they know His likes and dislikes, they should strive to please Him as much as possible, and avoid that which displeases Him.
4. It is obvious that there should be rewards for good deeds and punishments for evil doings, because equating good with bad is against justice and fair play.
5. But this world is not the place where a person's good or evil acts are recompensed in full. On the contrary, very often the opposite is seen: the evil-doers thrive very well in this world, while the one who abstains from evils suffers troubles and tribulations.
6. Therefore a time must come when this system comes to an end and a reckoning of everyone's good and evil acts takes place, with rewards and punishments awarded accordingly. That time is the Day of Judgment and the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the gist: had the disbelievers pondered these things, this very sky and earth and the creatures in between them would have testified that they are not permanent — they are here but for a short time, after which a new world is to come, which will be permanent.

Step 2 above is easy to skim past, but it is the practical heart of the whole passage. Reflection is not meant to end in wonder. It is meant to end in a question — *what does He like, and what does He dislike?* — and then in a change of behaviour.

**"And indeed many of mankind deny the meeting with their Lord."** After the argument comes the sober observation. What is denied is *the meeting* with their Lord — not an abstract "afterlife" but an encounter, standing before Him. And the ayah does not say "some"; it says *many*. This is the majority condition, not a fringe one — which is precisely why a believer cannot measure truth by counting heads.

Ibn Kathir adds that Allah then tells us of the truth of the Message brought by the Messengers, and how He supported them with miracles and clear signs — such as when He destroyed those who disbelieved in them and saved those who believed in them. That is the bridge into ayah 9.

## Ayah 9: get out on the road and look

**Who is being addressed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the invitation concrete. The Makkans live in a land where there is neither any cultivation and industry nor any tall and beautiful buildings — but for the sake of trade they *do* travel, to Syria and to Yemen. So the question is not asking them to do anything new. They are already on those routes. It only asks them to open their eyes while they are on them: during the course of those trips, have they not seen what was the fate of the earlier people?

Ibn Kathir broadens the sense so that no one can excuse himself for lack of a camel: *a-wa lam yasīrū fi'l-arḍ* means "do they not understand and think and see and hear about the people of the past?" Travel is the vivid form of it; the real command is to pay attention to what came before.

**What they would see.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the earlier nations as peoples whom Allah had endowed with skills to make use of the land: they had the skill to draw underground water by excavating the earth for irrigating fields and gardens, and to dig out concealed precious minerals such as gold and silver and make use of them to their benefit. For their advanced skills and way of living, they were regarded as civilized nations.

Ayah 9 puts it in two verbs, *athāru'l-arḍ wa ʿamarūhā*, which Ibn Kathir's rendering gives as "they tilled the earth and populated it in greater numbers than these have done." They worked the ground and they built on it, further than the Makkans ever had. These were not primitive people. They were the developed world of their day.

Ibn Kathir presses the comparison directly at the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries: the nations of the past who came before you were stronger than you to whom Muhammad ﷺ has been sent; they had more wealth and more sons; **you have not been given one-tenth of what they were given**; they stayed longer in this world than you will stay; they were more civilized than you and were more prosperous in the land than you.

**And then what happened.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues the story: they got engrossed so much in material life, transitory luxuries and comforts, that they forgot Allah and the Hereafter. Then Allah sent prophets and books to remind them of their duties, but they did not pay any heed. Ultimately they were overtaken by Allah's wrath even in this world, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the ruins of their desolate cities still stand witness to their destruction.

Ibn Kathir makes the same point with a chill in it: their Messengers came to them with clear signs while they were enjoying their life of luxury; Allah punished them for their sins and they had no one who could protect them from Allah. Their wealth and sons could not protect them from the wrath of Allah in the slightest.

Read that against the earlier nations' skills — the wells, the irrigation, the mines. Every capacity they had was a gift, and none of it was a defence.

## "Allah wronged them not — they wronged themselves"

This is the sentence the whole ayah has been building toward, and both commentaries stop on it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that at the end of the ayah it is suggested to ponder whether these nations were subjected to any oppression from Allah, or whether they subjected themselves to their own cruelty by accumulating causes of the divine punishment. Put that way, the answer is not in doubt. Nobody forced them to ignore the prophets.

Ibn Kathir says it plainly: Allah was not at all unjust towards them when He sent His punishment upon them — **they brought destruction upon themselves** when they rejected and mocked the signs of Allah. All of this, he adds, only happened because of their previous sins and their rejection of the Messengers.

Here is the divine justice the passage has been arguing for since ayah 8. If the universe was made *with truth*, then no punishment its Maker sends is arbitrary. The wrong in these ruins is real — but its author is the wrongdoer himself. Sin, in this picture, is above all self-harm.

## Ayah 10: the end of those who did evil

Ayah 10 closes the file: *Then evil was the end of those who did evil, because they denied the Ayat of Allah and made a mockery of them.*

Notice how the ayah pairs the deed with its outcome: those who did evil, and evil as their end. The recompense is not something foreign imported from outside; it is what their own conduct came to.

**Two readings of "because they denied."** Ibn Kathir preserves more than one way of reading the connection between the deeds and the end.

- He first sets the ayah alongside three others: *"And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe therein for the first time, and We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly"* (6:110); *"So when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away"* (61:5); *"And if they turn away, then know that Allah's will is to punish them for some sins of theirs"* (5:49). Placed beside those ayat, the picture is of wrongdoing that draws on further blindness — the turning away is answered by hearts being turned away, so that the hardening is itself part of the consequence.
- Then, he reports, "it was said" that the meaning is that evil was their **inevitable end, because** they rejected the signs of Allah and made fun of them — the denial being the cause, and the end its consequence. Ibn Kathir identifies this as the view of Ibn Jarir, which he recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah; Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it from them and from Ad-Dahhak bin Muzahim. Ibn Kathir adds that this is the apparent meaning — "and Allah knows best" — of the closing phrase, "and made a mockery of them."

Both readings hold the same warning from opposite ends: whether sin drags a person into denial, or denial drags him into ruin, the movement is downward and it is self-propelled.

**Mockery.** The ayah does not stop at denial; it adds that they "made a mockery" of the signs of Allah. Mockery is a step beyond argument. A man who argues against the truth is at least still engaging with it; a man who laughs at it has closed the door. Ibn Kathir names exactly this — rejecting and mocking the signs of Allah — as what brought destruction upon those magnificent civilisations.

## Living it

**Do the thinking the ayah asks for, and let it land somewhere.** Ayah 8 does not ask for admiration of nature; it asks for a conclusion. Following Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's chain: this was made on purpose → it has a fixed end → then justice must be settled somewhere → so learn what your Creator likes and dislikes, pursue the one and avoid the other. Reflection that never reaches that third step has stopped short of what the ayah wanted.

**Travel with your eyes open.** The Makkans were already going to Syria and Yemen for trade. Their failure was not that they never saw ruins; it was that they saw them and drew nothing from them. Whatever passes before your eyes — old powers, the wreckage of people who once looked untouchable — is meant to be read, not just viewed.

**Do not confuse capability with safety.** These nations had the strength, the skills, the wealth, the numbers. Ibn Kathir's line is worth keeping: you have not been given one-tenth of what they were given. Their skills came from Allah, and did not save them from Him.

**Beware the lopsided life.** Ibn Kathir records the words of Al-Hassan Al-Basri about people so absorbed in this world that "one of them could put a Dirham on his finger and tell how much it weighs, but he does not know how to pray properly." That is the disease of ayah 8 in a single image: sharp expertise about what is passing, careless ignorance about what is permanent. It is worth asking honestly which of the two describes our own attention.

**Never make light of the signs of Allah.** Ayah 10 names mockery alongside denial as what ended those nations. Guarding one's tongue — and one's laughter — around the verses of Allah, His commands, His Messengers and His religion is not a small piece of etiquette. In this passage, it is the line between a nation that survives and a nation whose ruins are all that is left of it.

passages.title: Resurrection and the parting of two groups
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat take the argument of the sūrah to its end point: the same Allah who began creation will bring it back, and the return is to Him. From that single premise the passage moves straight to the Day itself and shows what happens there — the collapse of every false support the guilty relied on, and then the final sorting of humanity into two groups who will never meet again.

What holds ayat 11–16 together is a movement from **power** to **verdict**. Ayah 11 establishes that resurrection is possible and certain. Ayat 12–13 show the guilty at that moment, stripped of help. Ayah 14 announces the separation. Ayat 15 and 16 give the two destinations — and the passage ends, deliberately, on the second.

## The premise: He who began it can bring it back (ayah 11)

*"It is Allah Who originates the creation, and will resurrect."*

Ibn Kathir's comment on this is one sentence, and the whole passage rests on it: **"Just as He was able to create it in the first place, so He is also able to repeat it."** This is not a mystical claim but an argument from the obvious. Whoever denies resurrection is not denying something harder than what has already, visibly, happened to him. He exists. He was originated. The One who did that once is not stretched by doing it again.

The ayah then adds the consequence: *thumma ilayhi turjaʿūn* — "then to Him you will be returned." Ibn Kathir explains this as the Day of Resurrection, **"when each will be requited according to his deeds."** So the return is not merely a re-assembling of bodies; it is a return to a reckoning. The ayah does not stop at establishing that Allah *can* raise the dead; it names where the raising leads.

## The guilty at that moment (ayah 12)

*"On the Day the Hour will arrive, the wicked will be dumbstruck."*

The Arabic verb here — *yublisu* — is difficult to carry into English in one word, and the earliest commentators reached for different sides of it. Ibn Kathir renders it as being **"plunged into destruction with despair."** He then reports:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "The sinners will be filled with despair."
- **Mujāhid**: "The sinners will be exposed" — and in another report from him, "The sinners will grieve."

These are not competing readings so much as three angles on one state. Despair is the inward collapse: there is nothing left to hope for. Exposure is the outward collapse: the cover is off, and what a person actually was is now public. Grief is what remains when both have happened. Put them together and you have the picture the English "dumbstruck" reaches for — a person with nothing to say, nothing to try, and nowhere to look.

Note also the word for the guilty, *al-mujrimūn*, which Ibn Kathir renders "the criminals" and elsewhere "the sinners." The passage is not describing people overtaken by bad luck. It is describing people who did something.

## The failure of the false intercessors (ayah 13)

*"There will be no intercessors for them from among their associate-gods…"*

Ibn Kathir is direct: **"the gods whom they used to worship instead of Allah will not intercede for them; they will reject them and betray them despite their desperate need of them."**

Sit with the sequence in that sentence. First, the failure — the objects of worship do nothing. Then the reversal — they *reject* those who worshipped them. Then the timing — this happens precisely at the moment of *"desperate need."* Everything a person spends a life investing in as a second line of defence beside Allah turns, on that Day, into a party to the prosecution rather than the defence.

The ayah's own wording completes the mutual disowning: they had made these things partners with Allah, and now, as Ibn Kathir's rendering of the verse has it, **"they will reject and deny their partners."** The relationship does not merely fail; it inverts.

Ayah 11 said that all origination and all return belong to Allah. Ayah 13 shows what it costs to have lived as though something else could stand in that place.

## The separation that has no reunion (ayah 14)

*"And on the Day the Hour will arrive, the people will then be separated."*

Read ayat 12 and 14 side by side and you will notice the Qur'an repeats the identical opening — *wa yawma taqūmu al-sāʿah*, "and on the Day when the Hour will be established." The repetition is not filler. The first time, the clause introduces what happens *inside* the guilty: despair. The second time, it introduces what happens *between* people: division. Same instant, two different cameras.

On the word *yatafarraqūn* — "they will be separated" — Ibn Kathir preserves a line from **Qatādah** that is hard to shake off once you have heard it:

> "By Allah, this refers to the separation after which there will be no reunion."

Ibn Kathir then draws out what that means: *"if one person is taken up to the highest heights and another is sent down to the lowest depths of Hell, that is the last they will ever see of one another."*

Every parting we know in this life is provisional. People move away, friendships lapse, and even death is, for the believer, a parting with a horizon on it. This one has no horizon. Qatādah swears by Allah precisely because the mind resists it — we assume, at some level, that everyone we love ends up somewhere near us. The ayah says the sorting is by *what people were*, not by whom they sat with, and once it is done it is permanent. That thought belongs in the mind of anyone choosing companions, choosing a spouse, raising children, or deciding how hard to work at calling the people they love toward good while there is still time.

## The first group: *yuḥbarūn* (ayah 15)

*"As for those who believed and did good, they will be rejoicing."*

Two things qualify the first group, and the ayah lists both: **belief** and **righteous deeds** — the inward assent and the life it produces.

Their reward is given in two words: they are *fī rawḍah*, in a garden, and *yuḥbarūn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the second word. *Yuḥbarūn* comes from ***ḥubūr***, which means happiness, joy, or delight. And then the crucial observation: **"This word encompasses all types of delight, which the dwellers of paradise will draw from the bounties of Paradise. The Holy Qur'an has not specified this, and has rather kept it generalized."**

That deliberate lack of specification is itself the point. Where a listing would have set a ceiling, the open word sets none. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports this by pointing to another ayah, 32:17, which it renders: *"no one knows in this world what delight and joy is in store for them (the people of Paradise) in Paradise."* Commentators, it notes, have mentioned various delightful things when explaining that verse, and all of them fall under the single heading of joy and delight — none of them exhausts it.

Ibn Kathir reports that **Mujāhid and Qatādah** glossed *yuḥbarūn* as: "they will enjoy a life of luxury." His own rendering of the ayah is that such people "shall be honored and made to enjoy a luxurious life in a Garden of Delight." Two elements sit there together — *honour* and *enjoyment*. The believer is not merely comfortable in Paradise; he is held in esteem there. After a life in which faith often costs status, that pairing is its own kind of answer.

## The second group (ayah 16)

*"And as for those who disbelieved, and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter…"*

Where ayah 15 named two qualities of the saved, ayah 16 names three of the ruined, and they build on one another: they **disbelieved**; they **denied Our āyāt** — the signs and revealed verses, the evidence that was actually put in front of them; and they denied **the meeting of the Hereafter** — the very thing ayah 11 had just established. The order runs from an inward refusal, to the rejection of what was sent, to the denial of the return itself. The passage has come full circle: it opened by asserting the return to Allah, and it closes by identifying those who called that assertion a lie.

Their end, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, is that **"such shall be brought forth to the torment"** — they do not wander into it; they are produced, presented, brought forward. It is a verdict being executed, not an accident.

## What the passage asks of us

**Take the argument of ayah 11 seriously.** Doubt about the Hereafter usually feels like sophistication. Ibn Kathir's answer treats it as a failure to think one step back: the One who was able to create in the first place is able to repeat it. And the repeating is not the end of it — the return is to Allah, "when each will be requited according to his deeds."

**Audit what you are leaning on.** Ayah 13 is a warning about anything we quietly expect to cover for us beside Allah. What does not help at that moment of "desperate need" — and, worse, turns and rejects the one who relied on it — is not worth what we pay for it now.

**Let ayah 14 shape your urgency.** Qatādah's oath — a separation with no reunion — is a reason to be serious about the people you love, and about which of the two groups your own daily life is enrolling you in.

**Do not measure Paradise by what you can picture.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about *ḥubūr* is liberating: the word was left open, and the Qur'an kept it generalized, because the reality is larger than any description. The believer's hope is not limited by the poverty of his imagination.

**And notice where the passage chooses to end.** It could have closed on the garden. It closes instead on those who denied the meeting with Allah and are brought forth to the torment. The last word is left with the warning — not to crush hope, but because the sorting in ayah 14 is permanent, and the time to be on one side of it is now.

---

### A note on context, from outside this passage

*The following comes from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's commentary on ayah 9, which precedes these six ayat. It is included as background to the sūrah's wider argument, not as commentary on ayat 11–16.*

Explaining *"Have they not travelled on earth"* (30:9), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Makkans lived in a land without cultivation, industry, or tall and beautiful buildings, but travelled for trade to Syria and Yemen. On those journeys they passed the remains of earlier peoples whom Allah had endowed with real skill: they could draw underground water by excavating the earth to irrigate fields and gardens, and dig out concealed precious minerals such as gold and silver and turn them to their benefit. For their advanced skills and way of living, the commentary says, they were regarded as civilized nations. And then: *"they got engrossed so much in material life, transitory luxuries and comforts that they forgot Allah Taʿālā and the Hereafter."* Allah sent prophets and books to remind them of their duties, *"but they did not pay any heed."* They were ultimately overtaken by Allah's wrath even in this world, and the ruins of their desolate cities still stand witness to their destruction. At the end of that verse, the commentary observes, we are invited to ponder whether they were subjected to any oppression from Allah — or whether they subjected themselves to their own cruelty by accumulating the causes of the divine punishment.

passages.title: Glorify Allah morning and evening
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take the ordinary turning of a day — dusk, dawn, late afternoon, high noon — and make each of those moments a summons. Allah commands that His purity be proclaimed and His praise be spoken as the sky changes; then, in ayah 19, He tells us what those changing skies are evidence of: the same power that brings the living out of the dead and revives dead earth is the power that will bring us out. That is what holds the passage together — worship in ayat 17–18, and the proof of resurrection in ayah 19, spoken as one breath.

## What "subḥān Allah" is actually saying

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with the word itself. **Subḥān** is an infinitive (a verbal noun) meaning "to declare the purity of someone from defects." So *subḥān Allah* is not a vague exclamation of wonder; it is a statement with content: **Allah is free of every defect.** To recite the phrase with that intention is what is called *tasbīḥ*.

There is a grammatical detail worth noticing in ayah 17. The verse does not begin with an ordinary command verb — it begins with the verbal noun *fa-subḥāna Llāh*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **a verb is understood before the infinitive**, and that understood verb is what directs the listener to make *tasbīḥ*. Ibn Kathir describes the same double movement from the other side: **here Allah glorifies Himself and commands His servants to glorify and praise Him.** The declaration and the command arrive together.

And *tasbīḥ*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is used in two ranges. Narrowly it is the phrase on the tongue. But **in general usage the word often includes all forms of worship and remembrance of Allah — salah, dhikr, and the like** — and it is this broader sense that is intended here. The verse itself never specifies the word *ṣalāh*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion directly: because prayer is not named as such, **all types of worship, "whether by actions or by word of mouth," are included in the meaning of the verse** — and since prayer is supreme among all acts of worship, it is included here on priority.

Ibn Kathir adds where these appointed moments come from: they are times **"which come one after the other and are indicative of His might and power in the heavens"** — the night arriving with its darkness, and then the morning arriving with its light.

## Four windows in the day — and where the fifth is

Ayah 17 names two times: *ḥīna tumsūn*, when you see the evening, and *ḥīna tuṣbiḥūn*, when you see the morning. Ayah 18 names two more at its close: *ʿashiyyan wa ḥīna tuẓhirūn*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines these last two carefully. **ʿAshiyy** is the name for the last part of the day, and here it refers to the time of **ʿAṣr**. The other is when **the sun starts declining towards the West — that is, Ẓuhr.** So the structure of the passage is: two times of remembrance at the start, and two more at the end, wrapped around the great statement of praise in between.

This is why Ibn Kathir heads this whole section **"The Command to pray Five Times Daily."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that scholars have stated that this verse has clearly described and defined the timings of the five prayers, and the clearest statement of that comes through a companion. **Someone asked Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) whether the Qur'an has specifically mentioned the five prayers.** He answered yes, and quoted this very verse as proof. Then, explaining his point, he said:

- **"when you see the evening"** (*ḥīna tumsūn*) — **Maghrib**
- **"when you see the morning"** (*ḥīna tuṣbiḥūn*) — **Fajr**
- **"in the afternoon"** (*ʿashiyyan*) — **ʿAṣr**
- **"and when you enter the time of Ẓuhr"** (*wa ḥīna tuẓhirūn*) — **Ẓuhr**

In this way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the verse has described four prayers very clearly. As for **ʿIshāʾ**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues that it is enjoined explicitly in the verse *min baʿdi ṣalāti l-ʿishāʾ* — "after the prayer of ʿIshāʾ" (24:58).

Here there is a second view, and it is worth knowing rather than flattening. **Sayyidnā Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may Allah have mercy on him) held the opinion that the words "when you see the evening" include both Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ** — in which case all five are in this passage itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports both. What both agree on is the substance: the hours of the daily prayers are written into these ayat.

## Why evening before morning, and ʿAṣr before Ẓuhr

The order is strange if you assume the verse is simply walking through a clock. Evening comes before morning; the end of the day (ʿAṣr) comes before midday (Ẓuhr). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a reason for each — and offers them modestly, as reasons rather than the only possible ones.

**Evening first:** one reason for the precedence of evening over morning is that **in the Islamic calendar evening precedes the morning, and the date changes at sunset (Maghrib).** On that reckoning the sequence is not out of order at all; it begins the day where the Islamic day itself begins.

**ʿAṣr before Ẓuhr:** one reason could be that at the time of ʿAṣr — **also called the middle (*wusṭā*) prayer** — **people are generally busy in their work, and so it is rather difficult to offer prayer at that time.** This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is why there is greater emphasis in the Qur'an on the ʿAṣr prayer: *ḥāfiẓū ʿalā ṣ-ṣalawāti wa ṣ-ṣalāti l-wusṭā* — "Take due care of all the prayers, and the middle prayer" (2:238). Mentioning it out of clock order puts a hand on the shoulder of the busiest hour of your afternoon.

## The praise that fills the heavens and the earth

Between the four time-markers sits ayah 18's great clause: *wa lahu l-ḥamdu fī s-samāwāti wa l-arḍ* — "And His is all the praise in the heavens and the earth."

Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: **He is the One who is to be praised for what He has created in the heavens and on earth.** Notice how the verse moves. First *tasbīḥ* — clearing Allah of every defect — and then, as Ibn Kathir puts it, **"this glorification is followed by befitting praise."** Every unworthy notion about Allah is cleared away first; the praise that follows is praise that befits Him.

And the scope is what makes the ayah so large. Your *tasbīḥ* has appointed hours in a day. But the praise named here belongs to Allah **in the heavens and the earth**, for everything He has created there.

Ibn Kathir then dwells on the two remaining time-words with real feeling. **ʿAshiyy is the time when the darkness is most intense; Iẓhār is the brightest point of the day.** The verse puts the deepest dark and the fiercest light side by side — and Ibn Kathir exclaims: **"Glory be to the One Who created both of them, the Cleaver of the daybreak and the One Who makes night a time of rest."** He shows that this pairing of dark and light as a sign of Allah runs right through the Qur'an, citing the oaths: *"By the day as it shows up its brightness. By the night as it conceals it"* (91:3–4); *"By the night as it envelops. By the day as it appears in brightness"* (92:1–2); *"By the forenoon. By the night when it darkens"* (93:1–2) — "and there are many similar Ayat."

So the times of prayer are not arbitrary slots. They are the moments Ibn Kathir describes as coming one after another and **"indicative of His might and power in the heavens."**

## Ayah 19: the argument hidden inside the day

Now the passage turns, and the turn is the whole point. *Yukhriju l-ḥayya mina l-mayyiti wa yukhriju l-mayyita mina l-ḥayy* — "He brings out the living from the dead, and brings out the dead from the living."

Ibn Kathir says this is **what we see of His power to create things and their opposites.** These ayat, coming one after the other, are all of the same kind: in each of them Allah mentions the creation of a thing and of its opposite, **"to indicate to His creation the perfection of His power."** His examples are deliberately ordinary — things you could watch happen:

- the plant from the seed, and the seed from the plant
- the egg from the chicken, and the chicken from the egg
- man from sperm, and sperm from man
- **the believer from the disbelievers, and the disbeliever from the believers**

That last pair carries the list beyond biology: the same "power to create things and their opposites" that Ibn Kathir sees in seed and plant, he sees also in belief and disbelief.

Then: *wa yuḥyi l-arḍa baʿda mawtihā* — "And He revives the earth after its death." Ibn Kathir gathers the passages where this same sign appears, and it is worth noticing where each of them ends up:

- "And a sign for them is the dead land. We give it life, and We bring forth from it grains, so that they eat thereof …" running to "and We have caused springs of water to gush forth therein" (36:33–34)
- "And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water on it, it is stirred, and it swells and puts forth every lovely kind" — running to: **"and certainly, Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves"** (22:5–7)
- "And it is He Who sends the winds as heralds of glad tidings, going before His mercy. Till when they have carried a heavy-laden cloud …" ending with **"so that you may remember or take heed"** (7:57)

And then the verse lands: *wa kadhālika tukhrajūn* — **"And thus shall you be brought out."**

*Thus.* Not some unimaginable new kind of act, but **like that** — the way the dead land is given life, the way you have already watched it happen every time a barren field stirred and swelled and put forth. The resurrection people find hard to accept is of a piece with what Allah has been doing in front of them all along; that is exactly why 22:5–7 moves from the reviving earth to those in the graves.

This is why ayat 17–18 and ayah 19 belong together. The hours of prayer sit on the day's transitions; those transitions are indicative of Allah's might and power. Every Maghrib and every Fajr, you are standing at the site of the proof.

## The dhikr of Ibrahim, and a report on its reward

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two things here that transform how these ayat feel.

First, a **Special Note**: this verse is the dhikr of **Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him)**, which earned him the title *wa Ibrāhīma lladhī waffā* — "and Ibrahim who fulfilled his covenant" (53:37). He used to recite these words in the morning and evening. And it is reported from **Sayyidnā Muʿādh ibn Anas (may Allah be pleased with him)**, with authentic proofs, that the reason behind awarding Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm the title of "fulfilling his covenant" was his recitation of this prayer.

Sit with that. The title of *the one who fulfilled* is tied to words he said every morning and every evening, without fail. Fulfilment, on this reading, has as much to do with never letting the hour pass unmarked as with the size of any single act.

Second, a report. **Abū Dāwūd, Ṭabarānī and Ibn as-Sunnī** have reported on the authority of **Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him)** that the Prophet ﷺ said — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān introduces it as what he said **"about these two verses,"** and then sets out 30:17–19 in full — **that whoever recites them in the morning, all shortcomings in his acts during the day will be repaired; and whoever recites them in the evening, all shortcomings in his actions during the night will be repaired.** (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from *Rūḥ*.)

That promise sits well with the ayat themselves. A shortcoming in a deed is a kind of deadness in it — and the passage being recited is precisely about the One who brings the living out of the dead.

## Living it

The passage asks for something small, timed, and repeatable.

**Guard the named hours.** They are Fajr, Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr and Maghrib in Ibn ʿAbbās's reading, with ʿIshāʾ enjoined explicitly at 24:58 — or, on Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's view, with ʿIshāʾ already folded into "the evening" here. Prayer is what this verse includes on priority.

**Give ʿAṣr the extra attention the ordering implies.** The verse mentions it out of sequence; the Qur'an calls it the middle prayer and tells you to take due care of it (2:238). It is difficult precisely because people are busy at that hour — and that difficulty is the reason for the emphasis, not an excuse against it.

**Do not let the verse shrink to the prayer alone.** Since the wording does not specify *ṣalāh*, all types of worship — by action or by word of mouth — are included in its meaning.

**Take up Ibrahim's habit.** Recite these ayat morning and evening, as Sayyidnā Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) used to, and as the report above describes, and let them do their repairing work on a day that will certainly have holes in it.

**And when you say them, look up.** These times were chosen because they are indicative of Allah's might and power. Say *subḥān Allah* while the light is actually going or actually coming, and *wa kadhālika tukhrajūn* stops being a doctrine you affirm and becomes something you are watching.

passages.title: Among His signs: creation, spouses, sleep, lightning
passages.tafsir:
**In brief:** six times over, Allah points to something so ordinary we walk past it daily — dust, marriage, a stranger's language, sleep, a flash of lightning, the sky staying up — and says: *this is one of My signs.* What binds ayat 20–25 into one unit is the refrain **وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ** ("and among His signs") at the head of every one of them, and the single conclusion all six are marshalled toward: the One with this power alone deserves worship, and the One who did all this can raise you again.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Sūrat al-Rūm opened with the war between Rome and Persia, then diagnosed the root of the disbelievers' heedlessness: excessive love of material life and no heed paid to the Hereafter. It described Allah's exclusive omnipotence, in which no one is His partner. The obvious conclusion, Maʿārif says, is that no one but Allah is entitled to be worshipped, and that what He has conveyed through His prophets about the Day of Judgement, resurrection, reckoning, Paradise and Hell must be believed in its totality.

These six ayat are the evidence for exactly that. Maʿārif counts them as **six manifestations of His omnipotence together with all-encompassing wisdom**. And it tells us how the six are wired together: the sixth (ayah 25) is "in fact the sum and substance of the previous five," which were revealed to explain and elaborate it. So read ayat 20–24 as five witnesses called to the stand, and ayah 25 as what they were called to establish — a universe held in place by His command, and a single call that empties the graves.

## Signs you can find without leaving your own house (ayat 20–21)

**"He created you from dust, then — behold — you are human beings scattered."**

Ibn Kathir: among His signs is that He created *your father Adam* out of dust. Then the arc of every one of us since: origins in dust, then a despised liquid, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bones in the form of a human being; then Allah clothes the bones with flesh, then the soul is breathed in and the creature can hear and see. Then he comes forth from his mother's womb small and weak — and the longer he lives the stronger he becomes, until he reaches the age where he builds cities and strongholds, travels to different lands and across the seas, earns a living and amasses wealth. Ibn Kathir breaks off into praise: glory to the One who enabled them to learn all kinds of skills for earning a living, and caused them to vary in their levels of knowledge and intellectual ability, in how handsome or plain, rich or poor they are.

Maʿārif presses on the choice of *material*. Man is the most distinguished of creatures, the ruler of the universe — and he is created from earth, the most inferior of the constituting elements of nature. Of the four well-known elements — water, fire, air and earth — the last has not the slightest sense, sensation or movement; all the others have at least some movement, but earth is devoid of even that.

Iblīs (Shaitan) stumbled precisely here. His arrogance misled him: he regarded himself superior to man because he is made of fire. What he failed to understand, Maʿārif says, is that greatness and superiority are *awarded* by Allah — He is free to award them to anyone He chooses. Nothing was ever owed to the raw material.

And "from dust" holds of us directly, not only through Adam: Maʿārif notes that every man or woman is formed from a fluid made up of various ingredients, and the origin of most of those ingredients is nothing but earth.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a report of Imam Ahmad from Abū Mūsā, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah created Adam from a handful taken from throughout the earth. Hence the sons of Adam vary as the earth varies, so they are white and red and black and colours in between, evil and good, easy-going or difficult — or something in between."* Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī, who said, "This Hadith is Hasan Sahih."

**"And among His signs is that He created for you wives from among yourselves, that you may find repose in them, and He has put between you affection and mercy."**

**"From among yourselves"**: Ibn Kathir explains it as "He created females of your own kind, to be wives for you," and links it to *"It is He Who has created you from a single person, and He has created from him his wife, in order that he might enjoy the pleasure of living with her"* (7:189) — which, he says, refers to Ḥawwāʼ, whom Allah created from Adam, from the short rib on his left. Then his argument: had Allah made all of Adam's progeny male and created the females from another kind — from jinn, say, or animals — there would never have been harmony between them and their spouses; there would have been revulsion, the spouses being of a different kind. Out of His perfect mercy He made their wives of their own kind, and created love and kindness between them. A man stays with a woman, Ibn Kathir observes, because he loves her, or because he feels compassion towards her once they have a child together, or because she needs him to take care of her.

Maʿārif adds the other half of the wonder: women are created in the same genus as men, yet there is a world of difference between them in build, appearance, looks, character, habits, morals and disposition — and even this creation, on its own, is an excellent example of His supreme power for anyone seeking to recognise Allah.

**لِتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا — "so that you may find tranquillity in them."** Maʿārif draws the point out: if you ponder, it becomes evident that all the requirements of men from women end up in drawing peace of mind, tranquillity and comfort. The Qurʼān has put all of that into one word.

**The total outcome of married life is peace of mind and comfort.** And this rest, Maʿārif adds, is founded on lawful marriage: probe the societies that developed illicit ways of living together outside that bond, and you will find their lives devoid of peace and tranquillity.

**Why love and mercy, and not just law.** That tranquillity, Maʿārif says, can only be achieved where there is mutual recognition of each other's rights and a sincere effort to fulfil them; demanding only one's own rights leads to domestic quarrels and shatters the peace. One route to securing those rights would have been legislation alone — prohibition, warning, prescribed punishment, as with other rights between people. It is common experience that people cannot be corrected by a set of laws alone, unless the laws are accompanied by the nurturing of *taqwā* — the fear of Allah — in the heart. That is why, whenever the Qurʼān gives injunctions about social life, it pairs them with *"Fear Allah."*

The bond between husband and wife is of such a delicate and sensitive nature that no law can ensure each gives the other their full due, and no court can do it full justice. It is for this reason, Maʿārif notes, that the Prophet ﷺ selected for the *khuṭbah* of the *nikāḥ* — the sermon delivered at the marriage ceremony — those verses of the Qurʼān that press on piety, the fear of Allah and the Hereafter. Only those qualities in the spouses can stand as guarantor for the fulfilment of mutual rights.

So Allah did not restrict conjugal rights to a legal and religious relationship at all. He made them a natural and emotional requirement, on the same pattern as parents and children: He filled parents' hearts with a love that compels them to protect their children more than their own selves, and put a degree of natural love in children's hearts for their parents. **"And He has created love and kindness between you."**

**مَوَدَّة and رَحْمَة.** The literal meaning of *wudd* and *mawaddah*, Maʿārif explains, is "liking," which results in love and affection. Two distinct words are used, and citing Qurṭubī, Maʿārif offers this reading: *mawaddah* may refer to the young years, when the two are drawn to one another with love and affection; *raḥmah* to old age, when the passions subside and compassion for each other takes over. Do not mistake the second for the loss of the first.

**One sign, "signs" in the plural.** The ayah closes, *"Surely in this there are signs for a people who reflect."* Maʿārif notices the oddity: only one sign was mentioned, yet the plural is used — because the conjugal relationship has many aspects and many benefits, religious and worldly, so that taken together this one relationship contains a number of signs of the divine omnipotence.

## Signs at every scale, from the galaxies to your own voice (ayat 22–23)

**"And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours."**

Ibn Kathir sketches the first item: the heavens with their vast height and brightness and the beauty of their stars and planets, and the earth with its density, its mountains, valleys, seas, plains, animals and trees. And alongside that cosmic scale the ayah sets *your* tongues and *your* colours. Ibn Kathir lists the languages known to him: Arabic, and the tongues of the Tatars, the Georgians, Romans, Franks, Berbers, Tou Couleurs (of Sudan), Ethiopians, Indians, Persians, Slavs, Khazars, Armenians, Kurds and others — "only Allah knows the variety of languages spoken among the sons of Adam."

As for "colours," Ibn Kathir reads it of appearance generally: from the time Allah created Adam until the Hour begins, every person has two eyes, two eyebrows, a nose, a forehead, a mouth and two cheeks — and none of them looks like another. There is bound to be some difference in posture, appearance or speech, whether apparent or so hidden it can only be noticed with careful observation.

Ibn Kathir's report had the sons of Adam varying as the earth varies; here that variation is spread across the map as languages and colours. Maʿārif brings it home: babies of different colour and hue are born to the same parents under the same circumstances.

Maʿārif also extends "tongues" beyond languages. Some languages are so far apart that there seems to be no link between them at all — and the word covers accents, pronunciations and the qualities of voices too. Allah's omnipotence has made every individual's voice distinguishable from every other; men's voices are clearly distinct from women's, children's from the aged — and yet the apparatus of speech, the tongue, the lips, the throat, is the same in all of us. Maʿārif answers the thought with praise: *tabāraka'Llāh aḥsan al-khāliqīn.*

**"And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty."**

Ibn Kathir: among His signs is the cycle of sleep He has created during the night and the day, when people are able to cease moving and rest, so that their tiredness and exhaustion will go away — and He has enabled you to seek to earn a living and to travel about during the day.

Maʿārif pauses on the wording. Elsewhere the Qurʼān describes sleep as something done at night and the earning of sustenance as an act of daytime; here *both* are placed in both. There is no contradiction: the major purpose of night is sleep, with some economic activity as a secondary function, and the case of daytime is the opposite — mainly work, with a little time given to rest and sleep. Both descriptions are correct, and Maʿārif adds that the laboured interpretations by which some commentators try to restrict sleep to night and earning to day are not called for.

**Why sleep proves anything.** Because it is a gift, not an achievement — not something one has to cultivate, but a natural gift bestowed by Allah on His creatures. Maʿārif's proof is one anybody can test: sometimes one cannot sleep despite making every possible arrangement for comfort, and sometimes even sleeping pills become ineffective; yet when Allah wills, people fall asleep on hard floors amid severe, oppressive heat.

The same principle runs through provision. Two people with equal opportunity, knowledge and intellect, putting in equal effort and skill, do not necessarily succeed equally; one earns more than the other, because Allah's wisdom decreed it so. Maʿārif's conclusion guards against a misreading in either direction: **one should try to earn a living through all the means available to him, and at the same time not ignore that the outcome of his endeavours depends on the will of Allah, who is the real Provider.** Sleeping and working are not opposed to asceticism or trust in Allah — they are the pattern He built into His creation.

## Signs that point past this world (ayat 24–25)

**"And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, for fear and for hope, and He sends down water from the sky, and therewith revives the earth after its death."**

Ibn Kathir explains the pairing: sometimes you fear the heavy rain and destructive thunderbolts that follow, and sometimes you feel hope, when you see the flash, that much-needed rain will come. Maʿārif says the same, adding that the rain which follows by His will gives rise to numerous types of vegetation.

Water reaches an earth that was barren, with nothing growing there, and — as Ibn Kathir quotes from elsewhere in the Qurʼān — *"it is stirred, and it swells and puts forth every lovely kind of growth"* (22:5). Ibn Kathir states the conclusion outright: **in this is a clear sign and proof of the resurrection and the coming of the Hour.** The ground under your feet has already been raised from the dead, on schedule, every year of your life.

**"And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then afterwards, when He will call you by a single call, behold, you will come out from the earth."**

Ibn Kathir reads this alongside *"He withholds the heaven from falling on the earth except by His leave"* (22:65) and *"Verily, Allah grasps the heavens and the earth lest they should move away from their places"* (35:41): they stand firm by His command to them and His subjugation of them — not by their own strength. Ibn Kathir records that whenever ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, swore an emphatic oath, he would say: *"No, by the One by whose command the heaven and the earth stand."*

Maʿārif adds: this strong arrangement has been working for thousands of years without the slightest depreciation — and when He commands its breakup, it will end in no time. Then, by the command of Allah, all the dead will assemble on the plain for the reckoning.

Ibn Kathir describes the Day of Resurrection, when the earth will be exchanged with another earth and the dead will come forth from their graves, brought back to life by His command and His call to them — and he lines up the parallels: *"On the Day when He will call you, and you will answer with His praise and obedience, and you will think that you have stayed but a little while!"* (17:52); *"But it will be only a single Zajrah. When behold, they find themselves on the surface of the earth alive after their death"* (79:13–14); *"It will be but a single Sayhah, so behold they will all be brought up before Us!"* (36:53).

Notice how economical the second creation is. The first, as Ibn Kathir laid it out at ayah 20, needed dust, a fluid, a clot, flesh, bones, the breathing of the soul, a womb, and years of growth. The second needs **one call**. That is Maʿārif's point about the sixth sign being the sum and substance of the other five: every one of them was showing you a power for which this is no strain at all.

## How each sign is sealed

The closing formulas are not interchangeable. Each seals its sign for a different faculty.

- **"Signs for a people who reflect"** (21) — the marriage sign, whose plural, as Maʿārif noted, opens onto many aspects and benefits at once.
- **"Signs for men of sound knowledge"** (22) — this ayah gathers sky, earth, the difference of languages and dialects, and the difference of human colour, all of which, Maʿārif says, can be recognised and understood with a little attention.
- **"Signs for a people who listen"** (23), which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as *who understand*. Maʿārif suggests why hearing in particular: lie down in comfort and sleep commonly takes you; put in effort in trade or service and a living comes. But the hand behind both is not seen by the ordinary eye — this reality is described by the prophets of Allah. So the sign benefits those who listen with care and accept it without obstinacy.
- **"Signs for a people who understand"** (24) — because, as Maʿārif notes, the mysteries of lightning and rain and the resultant growth of vegetation can be understood by those with intellect.

## Living it

- **Look again at what you walk past** — your body, your marriage, last night's sleep, this month's income, the sky that did not fall.
- **Judge your marriage by the standard the ayah sets** — by whether there is peace of mind in the house; and secure it, as Maʿārif says, by mutual recognition of each other's rights and sincere effort to fulfil them, with taqwā underneath.
- **Work hard and hold the outcome loosely.** Pursue a living by all the means available to you, and do not ignore that the result rests with the real Provider.
- **Take the four seals as an invitation.** Reflect, learn, listen, reason. The One by whose command the heavens and the earth stand can call you out of the earth with a single call.

passages.title: A parable against taking partners with Allah
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from **who owns everything** to **who deserves worship** — and they close the gap with an argument drawn from the listener's own life. Ayah 26 states Allah's total ownership; ayah 27 speaks of the One who begins the creation and repeats it, and of the highest description belonging to Him; ayah 28 sets before the idolaters a parable taken from their own households; ayah 29 speaks of why, having heard it, they still turn away. The thread holding them together is a single claim: nothing in existence stands beside Allah as a partner.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places ayah 26 as the **sixth sign of divine omnipotence** in this stretch of the surah, and makes an important observation about it: this sixth sign is "the sum and substance of the previous five signs" — the earlier signs were in fact revealed in order to explain and elaborate this one. The existence of the sky and the earth stands by the command of Allah. This strong arrangement has been working for thousands of years perfectly, without the slightest depreciation — and when He commands its breakup, it will end in no time at all. Then, again by His command, all the dead will assemble on the plain for the reckoning. Maʿārif adds that the subject of this ayah continues in the next few ayat — which is why the passage is best followed as a single argument unfolding, rather than four separate statements.

## "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth" (26)

Ibn Kathir explains the opening clause in a few words: **"He owns it, and it is enslaved to Him."** This is not ownership in the way a man owns a field — where the field existed before him and will outlast him. It is the ownership of the One to whom the thing belongs entirely.

Then comes the striking phrase: **كُلٌّ لَهُ قَانِتُونَ**, *kullun lahu qānitūn* — "all are obedient to Him." Ibn Kathir glosses *qānitūn* (the obedient, the humbly submissive) as: **they are humble before Him and submit to Him, whether willingly or unwillingly.**

That last phrase is worth pausing over. It draws a line through the whole of creation. There is a submission that is chosen — the believer who prays, gives, restrains himself. And there is a submission that is not optional at all: the body that ages, the lungs that stop when they are told to stop. On Ibn Kathir's reading, no one stands outside this; the only question left open is whether a person enters that submission willingly.

Notice also what this does to the argument that arrives in ayah 28. If everything in the heavens and the earth is owned by Allah and submissive to Him, then whatever is pointed to as a "partner" is itself Allah's property. A slave cannot be a co-owner of the master's estate. The refutation is already embedded in the first ayah of the passage.

## Beginning, repeating, and what "easier" means (27)

**"And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him."**

Ibn Kathir heads this section plainly: *Repeating the Creation is easier for Allah*. The ayah sets the two acts side by side — the beginning and the repeating — and calls the second the easier of the two. Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities on the words *wa huwa ahwanu ʿalayh*:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (through the report of Ibn Abi Talhah): "This means it is easier for Him."
- **Mujahid**: "Repeating it is easier for Him than originating it — **and originating it is easy for Him**." This was also the view of **ʿIkrimah** and others.

Mujahid's second clause is the key that keeps the first from being misunderstood. He does not leave room for the idea that the first creation was taxing. Origination was already easy; repetition is easier still.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir brings here a hadith recorded by **Al-Bukhari** from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah says:

> "The son of Adam denied Me, and he had no right to do so. And he reviled Me, and he had no right to do so. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: 'He will not remake me as He originated me' — while originating the creation is not easier for Me than re-creating him. As for his reviling Me, it is his saying: 'Allah has taken to Himself a son,' while I am the One, the Self-Sufficient Master; I beget not, nor was I begotten, and there is none comparable to Me."

Ibn Kathir notes this was **recorded only by Al-Bukhari**.

Read the hadith alongside the ayah and the picture becomes precise. The ayah places the repeating and the originating in the order a human being naturally reasons in — of course redoing is easier than doing. The hadith speaks from Allah's own side and closes the door on the wrong inference: the first creation is *not* easier for Him than the second. The vocabulary of "harder" and "easier" simply does not apply to His power in the way it applies to ours.

The hadith also does something that fits this passage exactly. It names **two** offences of the son of Adam — denying that he will be remade, and saying that Allah has taken a son. These correspond to the two subjects the ayat are handling: the repeating of the creation in ayah 27, and the ascribing of partners in ayah 28.

## "His is the highest description in the heavens and in the earth" (27)

Then: **وَلَهُ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَىٰ**, *wa lahu al-mathal al-aʿlā*.

**The word itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up *mathal*: the word is used for anything that bears resemblance or similarity to something else — though being *exactly* like that thing is not necessary. The Qur'an therefore uses *mathal* of Allah in several places, including this ayah, and yet, as Maʿārif states, Allah's Being is completely beyond resemblance. That is why Maʿārif renders the phrase not as "the highest likeness" but as **"the highest attribute,"** which is also a possible lexical meaning of the word. The point matters for creed: the ayah is not offering a comparison for Allah.

**The scholars.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas (through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) that this phrase is like the ayah **"There is nothing like Him"** (42:11). And **Qatadah** said: "His description is *lā ilāha illallāh* — and there is no Lord but He."

Both readings are worth holding together. Ibn ʿAbbas reads it alongside a statement of transcendence: nothing is like Him. Qatadah reads it as content: the description of Allah is that there is no god but He. That is the sentence the whole passage is built to produce, and it lands right before the parable that demolishes its opposite.

## The parable drawn from your own lives (28)

**"He sets forth for you a parable from yourselves."**

Ibn Kathir explains *min anfusikum* — from yourselves — as meaning: **something which you yourselves can see, witness, and understand.** The argument reaches into an arrangement the listener lives inside every day, and lets him pass the verdict himself.

The parable: *Do you have partners among those whom your right hands possess, to share as equals in the wealth We have bestowed on you, whom you fear as you fear each other?*

Ibn Kathir unpacks it clause by clause:

- On "partners among those whom your right hands possess to share as equals": **"None of you would like to have his servant as a partner in his wealth, each of them having an equal share."**
- On "whom you fear as you fear each other": **"You fear that they will have a share in your wealth with you."**
