**Abu Mijlaz** adds the sharpened form of the argument: "You do not fear that your servant will have a share in your wealth, because he has no such right; similarly, Allah has no partner."

Ibn Kathir states the conclusion plainly: **since any one of you would abhor such a thing, how can you attribute rivals to Allah from among His creation?** A man will not accept his own servant as an equal partner in property he merely received. Yet partners are assigned to Allah from among the very creation that, as ayah 26 has already said, He owns and that is enslaved to Him.

**The context Ibn Kathir supplies.** Ibn Kathir describes this as a parable Allah makes of the idolaters — those who worship others besides Him and attribute partners to Him **while at the same time admitting that these so-called partners, idols and false gods, are enslaved to and belong to Him.** In their *talbiyah* — the chant they raised during Hajj and ʿUmrah — they used to say: *"At Your service, You have no partner **except the partner that You have — You own him and whatever he owns.**"*

Ibn Kathir brings a report recorded by **At-Tabarani** from Ibn ʿAbbas to the same effect: the people of shirk used to say this in their talbiyah, and then Allah revealed the words of this ayah. Sit with the self-contradiction. They admitted out loud, in the act of pilgrimage itself, that the partners they worshipped were owned by Allah. And it did not stop them.

Ibn Kathir draws out the conclusion: if human beings have this characteristic — this refusal to share ownership with a subordinate — then the parable shows it is even less befitting for Allah to have a partner.

**"Thus do We explain the signs in detail to a people who have sense."** The signs have been laid out in *detail*, one by one; the ayah addresses those who use their reason. Which sets up the last ayah.

## Why the argument does not land (29)

If the case is that clear, why is anyone still an idolater?

**"Nay, but those who do wrong follow their own lusts without knowledge."** Ibn Kathir identifies "those who do wrong" — *alladhīna ẓalamū* — as **the idolaters**, and their "lusts" (*ahwāʾahum*, their desires) as referring to **their worship of false gods without knowledge**. Just before this, commenting on "a people who have sense," Ibn Kathir says the idolaters worship others instead of Allah **"out of their own folly and ignorance."**

Note what has been diagnosed. On Ibn Kathir's reading the driver is desire and ignorance, not evidence. That is why a parable of this clarity can be recited to a man and change nothing.

**"Then who will guide him whom Allah has sent astray?"** Ibn Kathir: **no one can guide them if Allah has decreed that they will be misguided.**

**"And for such there will be no helpers."** Ibn Kathir: there is **no one who can save them from the power of Allah or grant them a way out — for what He wills, happens; and what He does not will, does not happen.** The false partners for whom a man abandoned tawhid cannot, in the end, stand up for him.

## Living it

**Check what you have quietly made a partner.** The talbiyah Ibn Kathir records is a warning about how comfortable a contradiction can become: they said aloud that their partners were owned by Allah, and kept them anyway. A person can affirm *lā ilāha illallāh* and still let something owned — a reputation, a salary, a fear of what people will say — take the decisive vote in his life.

**Argue with yourself the way ayah 28 argues.** Its method, in Ibn Kathir's words, is to work from something you can see, witness, and understand. You would not hand an equal share of what you own to someone who owns nothing except through you. Then weigh what you assign to Allah, who owns you.

**Let the raising of the dead sit as it sits in the ayah.** The One who begins the creation repeats it, and — as Mujahid says — the originating was already easy for Him. The hadith recorded by Al-Bukhari treats the denial of it as something far graver than a mistake: it calls it *denying* Allah, and pairs it with reviling Him.

**When someone does not accept a clear proof, remember ayah 29.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is sobering: no one can guide the one Allah has decreed will be misguided. So present the truth well — and then ask Allah for the heart of the one you are speaking to, and for your own.

passages.title: The upright faith and human primordial nature
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These three ayat are the practical conclusion of the argument about the Oneness of Allah that runs before them. Having shown how unreasonable it is to give Allah partners, the passage issues a command: face this one religion squarely, because it is the very nature Allah designed you upon — then live that out through turning back to Him, taqwa (being mindful of Allah and fearing Him), prayer, sincere worship of Him alone, and refusal to fracture into rival parties.

The three ayat are a single movement: **ayah 30** establishes the religion and its foundation in human nature; **ayah 31** gives the acts that keep a person on it; **ayah 32** shows the ditch on the other side of the road — what happens to people who alienate themselves from that original nature.

## The argument these ayat answer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what came just before. Allah had put a question to the idolaters drawn from their own lives: your servants and slaves are identical with you in looks, appearance, and their makeup of limbs and other physical features — yet you would never let them share your power and authority as equals. You are not willing to part with the slightest portion of your wealth and power in their favour. They can neither spend wealth nor time as they like, the way you do. So pause and ponder: human beings, angels, and everything else in the universe are created by Allah, all of them His creation and His slaves. How then could you take them as His equals or partners?

The following ayah then sounds a warning — the argument is simple and straightforward, yet there are people who, under the influence of their selfish motives, do not accept or concede anything of wisdom and knowledge.

So ayah 30 lands as the verdict: **since the irrationality and injustice of shirk (associating partners with Allah) has been established, leave aside all trends of shirk and turn to this faith with full devotion.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Prophet ﷺ is addressed here, and through him the entire human race.

## "So set your face" — the force of the command

*Fa-aqim wajhaka li-d-dīn ḥanīfā.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "So, set your face to the Faith steadily." Ibn Kathir gives the sense as: *set your face and persevere in the religion which Allah has prescribed for you* — and he immediately says what that religion is: **the worship of Allah alone, the religion of Ibrahim**, to which Allah has guided you and which He has perfected for you with the utmost perfection. In this manner, Ibn Kathir adds, you will also adhere to the sound fiṭrah with which He created His creation.

Ibn Kathir cites a narration in which Allah says: **"I created my servants *ḥunafā'* — that is, monotheists — then the Shayāṭīn misled them from their religion."** He then notes that Allah created His creation with the fiṭrah of Islam, and that afterwards corrupt religions such as Judaism, Christianity and Zoroastrianism emerged among some of them.

That is the hinge of the passage: monotheism is the original condition; deviation is a later interference.

## *Fiṭrah* — the design you were made on

*Fiṭrat Allāh allatī faṭara an-nāsa ʿalayhā* — "the *fiṭrah* of Allah upon which He created mankind," or, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering, "this faith being the nature designed by Allah on which He has created mankind." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the commentators assign different grammatical constructions to this sentence, but they all agree on one thing: **"the nature designed by Allah" refers back to the "straight Faith" that the first sentence commanded.** The clause is an elucidation of the first command, mentioning a special trait of this faith — that Islam is the religion of nature.

Ibn Kathir puts the same point in creedal terms: **Allah created His creation to recognise Him and to know His Tawhid, and that there is none worthy of worship except Him.** He links this to the primordial covenant in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, where Allah "made them testify as to themselves: *Am I not your Lord?* They said: *Yes!*" (7:172). The knowledge of Allah is not imported into a person from outside. It is native.

## "No change in Allah's creation" — how the scholars read it

*Lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh.* Ibn Kathir records more than one reading.

**First**, some said it means: *do not change the creation of Allah* — for if you do, you will divert people away from the fiṭrah with which He created them. So the statement carries instruction. Ibn Kathir compares it to the ayah "and whoever enters it, he is safe," and calls this **"a good and correct interpretation."**

**Second**, others said it means Allah made all of His creation equal: **all of them have the same sound fiṭrah and are by nature upright; they are all born with this nature, and there is no disparity among people in this regard.**

**Third**, Ibn Kathir lists a roll-call of early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibrahim an-Nakhaʿi, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥak and Ibn Zayd — who all said that "no change let there be in Allah's *khalq*" means **the religion of Allah**. And al-Bukhari said of this phrase: "It means the religion of Allah, and the religion, and the *fiṭrah* is Islam."

Then comes *dhālika d-dīn al-qayyim* — "that is the straight religion." Ibn Kathir explains: **adherence to the Sharīʿah and the sound fiṭrah is the true, straight religion.** Revelation and inborn nature are not rivals; the straight religion is where the two meet.

The ayah closes: *but most people do not know.* Ibn Kathir reads this as most people neither knowing this nor living by it, deviating far astray from it — and he sets alongside it two other ayat: "And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly" (12:103), and "And if you obey most of those on the earth, they will mislead you far away from Allah's path" (6:116). **Majority is not evidence.**

## From the Sunnah: the hadith of the newborn

Al-Bukhari reported that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"No child is born except in a state of fiṭrah, then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian or a Zoroastrian — just as each animal produces a perfect animal like itself. Do you see any among them that are born mutilated?"**

Abu Hurayrah then recited this very ayah: *"Allah's fiṭrah with which He has created mankind. No change let there be in Allah's khalq. That is the straight religion."* Ibn Kathir notes it was **also recorded by Muslim.**

Deviation from tawhid is not something a person arrives with.

## What exactly does *fiṭrah* mean? A real difference among the scholars

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works through this carefully, because two interpretations are current.

**The first:** *fiṭrah* here means Islam itself — that is, Allah made all human beings Muslim by their nature and instinct, so that all humans are born Muslims, and it is the surroundings and environment they live in that lead them astray. Commonly the parents teach the child beliefs contrary to Islam, and so he is misled into wrong belief. **According to Qurtubi, the majority of the elders agree with this interpretation**, and it is also recorded in a hadith of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, quoted above.

**The second:** *fiṭrah* means **capability** or **capacity** — Allah has bestowed on every human being the capability to discern his Creator and believe in Him, a capability that leads automatically to submission to Islam **provided one makes use of this divine grace.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then raises four difficulties with taking *fiṭrah* to mean Islam outright:

1. This very ayah says **"there is no change in Allah's creation"** — and "Allah's creation" here means the same as "the nature designed by Allah" mentioned earlier in the ayah. Yet the hadith of the two Ṣaḥīḥs says the parents make the child a Jew or a Christian. If *fiṭrah* means Islam, and no change in it is possible, how does that change occur? And it plainly does occur as a matter of common experience: there are more disbelievers in the world than Muslims.
2. An authentic hadith about the boy killed by Sayyidnā Khaḍir (peace be upon him) states that infidelity was embedded in his nature, and that this was why Khaḍir killed him — which is hard to square with all children being born upon Islam.
3. If Islam were embedded in human nature such that a person had no control to change it, it would not be a **voluntary** act — and in that case there would be no room for reward in the Hereafter, since reward is awarded for voluntary good deeds.
4. The religious jurists deduced from authentic ahadith that a child before attaining puberty is treated **in this world** according to the faith of his parents: if the parents are disbelievers the child is taken as such, and if he dies a minor he is not buried according to Islamic rites.

**Imam Torapushti** listed all these doubts in his commentary on the *Maṣābīḥ* and, because of them, preferred the second interpretation. And that reading resolves them: natural capability genuinely cannot be changed. The one who is misled by his parents into disbelief **does not lose his instinct to discern and comprehend Islam.** Even in the case of the boy killed by Khaḍir, it is not true that he had lost the capability to discern the truth. And since a person makes use of this divine gift by his own free will, the ground for reward is quite evident. The hadith of the two Ṣaḥīḥs then becomes clear: the child is born with the natural instinct to discern the truth, yet his surroundings and parents make him a Jew or a Christian.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also takes up the reports from some of the early authorities (*salaf*) who explained the word *fiṭrah* with the word "Islam," reading them in the light of this discussion of capability, and notes that **Muḥaddith Dehlavi** explained the view of the majority of the Ummah in the same manner.

**Shah Waliullah Dehlavi** endorsed the same view in *Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bāligha*: Allah has created innumerable things of various temperaments and dispositions, and has placed in the nature of each one an inherent quality that helps it fulfil the object of its creation. The ayah "He who gave everything its shape, then guidance" (20:50) describes this same reality — the Creator has instructed every creature how to fulfil the purpose of its creation, and those instructions are embodied in its own capabilities. The honeybee is given the instinct to distinguish plants and flowers, to make its selection, to draw the juice from them and store it in the hive. **In the same way, human beings are graced with a natural instinct and capability to recognise their Creator and submit to Him. This is what Islam is all about.**

The same lens clarifies "I have not created jinn and mankind except to worship Me" (51:56): Allah has created in their nature the inclination towards, and the capability for, His worship — and if they make use of that capability, they will never go wrong and astray.

It also settles *lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh*: **no one can bring about any change in the instinct and capability bestowed by Allah which helps a person recognise the truth. A wrong environment can make one a disbeliever, but it cannot eliminate his inherent capability to recognise the truth.**

## Ayah 31: four things that keep you there

Ayah 31 gives the practical shape of the upright faith. Ibn Kathir takes each phrase:

- **"Turning in repentance to Him"** (*munībīna ilayh*) — **Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jurayj said this means returning to Him.** The word describes a settled posture, a life spent coming back rather than a single act.
- **"And have taqwa of Him"** — Ibn Kathir: **fear Him, and remember that He is always watching.**
- **"And perform the Salah"** — which Ibn Kathir calls **the greatest act of worship.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the link back to ayah 30: since human nature is designed with an inherent capability to accept the truth, the establishment of prayer is **the first requisite for the acceptance of truth — the manifestation of submission to truth and the practical affirmation of faith in Islam.**
- **"And be not of the idolaters"** — Ibn Kathir: be of those who single out Allah, **devoting their worship sincerely for Him alone**, not to anyone or anything other than Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds why the idolaters are the counter-example: **they did not avail themselves of their natural capability to accept the truth.**

Ibn Jarir recorded that Yazid bin Abi Maryam said that **ʿUmar** (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by **Muʿadh bin Jabal** and asked, "What is the foundation of this Ummah?" Muʿadh said: "Three things, and they are the things that will bring salvation — **al-Ikhlāṣ**, doing a deed for Allah alone, which is the fiṭrah with which Allah created mankind; **Salah**, which is the thing that tells a believer apart from a disbeliever; and **obedience**, which is protection." ʿUmar said: "You have spoken the truth."

## Ayah 32: how a single nature becomes a hundred parties

Ayah 32 identifies the idolaters of ayah 31: *those who split up their religion and became sects, each sect rejoicing in that which is with it.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them as people who have created a difference between the natural faith and the true religion, and so are divided into different sects.

**On the wording.** Ibn Kathir explains *farraqū dīnahum* as **splitting up the religion — changing it by believing in parts of it and rejecting other parts.** He notes that **some scholars read it as *faraqū dīnahum***, meaning "neglected their religion and left it behind them." He identifies those described as being like the Jews, Christians, Zoroastrians, idol worshippers and all the followers of false religions besides the followers of Islam, citing "Verily, those who divide their religion and break up into sects, you have no concern in them in the least. Their affair is only with Allah" (6:159).

**On *shiyaʿan*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word: it is the plural of *shīʿah*, and **a group of people following a leader is called a *shīʿah*.** The natural faith was based on the Oneness of Allah, and by following it **the entire human race should have been one solid unit and one party.** Instead people split out from this unity and started following the personal views of their own leaders — and since personal views and opinions vary from person to person, different groups invented their own beliefs and their own religion. So people were divided into various groups and sects. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Shayṭān made each of them believe **they were the only people on the right path.**

**On *kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim fariḥūn*** — "each group is happy with what it has before it." **Each group is happy and contented in its own beliefs and declares the others wrong, although all of them are astray and treading the wrong path.** Delight in one's own group is presented not as evidence of truth but as a symptom of the disease.

Ibn Kathir applies it soberly to us too: the followers of the religions before us had differences of opinion and split into false sects, **each group claiming to be following the truth** — and this Ummah too has split into sects, all of which are misguided apart from one, **Ahlus-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah**: those who adhere to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and what was followed by the first generations — the Companions, their followers, and the Imams of the Muslims of earlier and later times. Ibn Kathir notes that **al-Hakim recorded in his *Mustadrak*** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked which of the sects was the saved sect, and he said: **"What I and my Companions are upon."**

## Living it

**Guard the environment around your fiṭrah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a practical ruling out of *lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh*: although the sentence is in the form of information, **it also contains a latent prohibition, in the sense that this nature should not be tampered with.** From this it is inferred that one **should avoid the situations that render the capability of accepting the truth ineffective or weak.** The commentary names where that damage typically comes from: **an evil environment, bad company, and reading books written by those having wrong beliefs — especially when the reader does not have extensive knowledge and information about Islam.** Your inborn capacity cannot be destroyed, but it can be buried under noise. Choose the noise you live in.

**Do not measure truth by numbers.** Ayah 30 ends by saying most people do not know — and Ibn Kathir reinforces it with 12:103 and 6:116.

**Keep the four commands of ayah 31 running.** Return to Him again and again, live aware that He is always watching, establish the prayer, and keep your worship sincerely for Him alone. Muʿadh's three — sincerity, prayer, obedience — are the same list from the inside.

**Beware the pleasure of belonging.** Ayah 32 warns against a party's delight in itself. If your religion has become mainly the satisfaction of being in the right group, this ayah is addressed to you. The remedy Ibn Kathir gives is not to find a better party but to hold to the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, and what the first generations followed.

passages.title: Crying in hardship, ungrateful in ease
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat hold up a mirror to the human heart and show us how unsteady it is: pressed by pain it calls on Allah alone, and released into comfort it forgets Him — sometimes to the point of setting up partners beside Him. Ibn Kathir titles this whole passage in one line: **"How man sways between Tawhid and Shirk, and between Joy and Despair, according to His Circumstances."** *Tawhid* means holding Allah to be One and worshipping Him alone; *shirk* is its opposite — associating someone or something with Allah in worship. That swinging between the two is what binds ayat 33 to 37 into a single unit. Ayah 33 gives the swing in terms of belief (hardship brings sincerity, ease brings the setting up of partners); ayah 36 gives the same swing in terms of mood (mercy brings elation, affliction brings despair); ayah 34 delivers the warning, ayah 35 strips away the excuse, and ayah 37 offers the cure — seeing the hand of Allah behind both the wide provision and the narrow one.

## Ayah 33: the emergency prayer

"And when harm touches men, they cry sincerely only to their Lord, turning to Him in repentance; but when He gives them a taste of His mercy, behold, a party of them associates partners in worship with their Lord."

Ibn Kathir's comment is simple and devastating: **when man is in dire straits, he calls upon Allah alone with no partner or associate; then when times of ease come and they have the choice, some people associate others with Allah and worship others alongside Him.**

Notice the phrase *and they have the choice*. Hardship is honest — it leaves a person with nothing but the call to the One who can actually help. Ease is where the test really lies, because in ease a person has options again, and it is his free choice — not his desperation — that reveals what he truly believes.

**"Turning to Him" (munībīn).** The Arabic *munībīn ilayhi* is rendered here as *turning to Him in repentance*. That is what makes the reversal in the second half of the ayah so painful: the very people described as turning back to their Lord are the ones who, once relieved, turn away again.

**"A party of them" (farīqun minhum).** Allah does not say all of them. Ibn Kathir keeps the same precision — *some people* associate others with Allah. The Qur'an is diagnosing a tendency in humanity, not condemning every human being; Ibn Kathir will state the exception plainly when he reaches ayah 36.

## Ayah 34: the warning that should stop us cold

"So as to be ungrateful for the graces which We have bestowed on them. Then enjoy; but you will come to know."

The ayah runs straight on from that turning away to its result: *li-yakfurū bimā ātaynāhum* — "so as to be ungrateful for the graces which We have bestowed on them." The gift itself becomes the occasion of the ingratitude. Then, says Ibn Kathir, **"Allah warns them"** with the words *fa-tamattaʿū fa-sawfa taʿlamūn* — "Then enjoy; but you will come to know."

There is no detail in that warning, and that is the whole force of it. Nothing is spelled out — only *you will come to know*. Ibn Kathir records that one of them said, on this phrase:

> "By Allah, if a law enforcement officer were to say this to me, I would be afraid — so how about when the One Who is issuing the warning is the One Who merely says to a thing 'Be!' and it is?"

That is the measure of the thing. An open-ended threat from a man with limited power is enough to keep us awake at night. Here the One saying *you will come to know* is the One whose word alone brings a thing into existence. "Then enjoy" is not permission; it is the calm of absolute power, letting a person run to the end of his rope.

## Ayah 35: no evidence was ever sent down

"Or have We revealed to them an authority, which speaks of that which they have been associating with Him?"

Having exposed the behaviour, Allah now removes its justification. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here **denounces the idolators for fabricating lies and worshipping others instead of Him with no evidence or proof.** He glosses the key words:

- *sulṭān* — translated "an authority" — **means proof**.
- *fa-huwa yatakallam* — "which speaks" — **means tells**.
- *bimā kānū bihi yushrikūn* — "of that which they have been associating with Him."

And Ibn Kathir names the rhetorical form exactly: **"This is a rhetorical question intended to denounce them, for they have no such thing."** The question is asked precisely because the answer is empty. No proof was ever sent down authorising anyone to be worshipped beside Allah. So shirk is not merely wrong; it is unsupported — a claim with nothing standing behind it.

## Ayah 36: the same instability, now in the emotions

"And when We cause mankind to taste of mercy, they rejoice therein; but when some evil afflicts them because of what their hands have sent forth, behold, they are in despair!"

Ayah 33 traced the swing in a person's *worship*. Ayah 36 traces it in a person's *inner state*, and the shape is identical. Ease no longer produces gratitude but a self-satisfied elation; hardship no longer produces prayer but collapse.

Ibn Kathir calls this **"a denunciation of man for the way he is, except for those whom Allah protects and helps."** Hold on to that exception; it is the door out of the passage.

**The rejoicing is not innocent joy.** Ibn Kathir explains that when man is given blessings **he is proud**, and he brings as illustration Allah's words in Surah Hud: *"Ills have departed from me." Surely, he is exultant, and boastful* (11:10). Ibn Kathir unpacks it in two directions: **he rejoices over himself and boasts to others.** Inwardly he concludes the trouble is behind him for good; outwardly he displays it. This is why the rendering "they become prideful" sits so naturally beside Ibn Kathir's "they rejoice therein": the fault is not the happiness, it is the swagger and the forgetfulness inside the happiness.

**And the despair is not sober grief.** The word the ayah uses for their reaction, *yaqnaṭūn*, is explained by Ibn Kathir in terms of a shut door: **when difficulties befall him, he despairs of ever having anything good again.** Not *this is hard*, but *nothing good will ever come to me again*.

**"Because of what their hands have sent forth."** The ayah itself supplies part of the explanation for the affliction — *bimā qaddamat aydīhim*. What arrives has a link to what was sent ahead. This is said of the people the ayah is denouncing.

**The exception.** Immediately after quoting 11:10, Ibn Kathir cites the words that follow it in Surah Hud: *Except those who show patience and do righteous good deeds* — and he defines them with a beautiful symmetry: **"They are patient during times of difficulty and do good deeds at times of ease."** That single sentence is the antidote to the whole passage. The unstable man is unstable because each state pulls a different vice out of him. The believer answers each state with a virtue: hardship is met with patience, ease is met with obedience.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir supports this with a hadith he reports as **"reported in the Sahih"**:

> "How wonderful is the affair of the believer. Allah does not decree anything for him but it is good for him. If good things happen to him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if bad things happen to him, he bears that with patience, and that is good for him."

This is the exact inverse of ayah 36. For the man described there, both states are a loss: ease costs him his humility and hardship costs him his hope. For the believer, both states are a gain, because he brings the right response to each — thanks in one, patience in the other. The decree does not change; what changes is the man receiving it. And notice how unrestricted the promise is: *Allah does not decree anything for him but it is good for him.*

## Ayah 37: the cure is to look

"Do they not see that Allah expands the provision for whom He wills and straitens it for whom He wills? Verily, in that are indeed signs for a people who believe."

The passage ends not with more rebuke but with an invitation to notice something. Ibn Kathir's comment on the widening and narrowing of *rizq* (provision — everything Allah allots a person to live on) goes straight to the point: **"He is the One Who is controlling and doing that, by His wisdom and justice, so He expands the provision for some people and restricts it for some."**

Three things follow from that, and together they dismantle everything the earlier ayat described:

**Wealth is not a verdict.** If both the abundance and the restriction come from the same wise and just Lord, then a full hand is not proof that Allah is pleased with you, and an empty one is not proof that He has abandoned you. The boasting and the despair of ayah 36 are both built on misreading one's own circumstances as a scorecard.

**There is no room for a partner.** The One who alone widens and narrows provision is the only One worth calling on — in the emergency of ayah 33 and equally in the comfort that follows it.

**Despair has no ground to stand on.** The One who straitened can expand. The man who concludes he will never see good again has forgotten who is holding the measure.

And then the closing phrase: **"Verily, in that are indeed signs for a people who believe."** The signs are public — everyone watches fortunes rise and fall — but they only register as *signs* for those who believe. The unstable man in this passage sees the same economy, the same illnesses, the same recoveries, and reads nothing in them.

## Living it

- **Watch what you do in ease, not only in hardship.** By Ibn Kathir's reading, it is in ease — when a person has the choice — that what he really believes comes out. The prayer that came easily during the crisis is the one to keep making when the crisis lifts.
- **Do not let a gift become the reason for ingratitude.** That is the precise charge in ayah 34: ungrateful *for the graces which We have bestowed on them*. Name the Giver when the gift arrives.
- **Refuse the sentence "nothing good will ever come to me again."** Ayah 36 names that despair, and ayah 37 answers it: the One who narrowed can widen.
- **Check what your certainty rests on.** Ayah 35 asks whether any authority — any proof — was ever sent down for worshipping another beside Allah. Ibn Kathir's answer is that the question is asked to denounce them, "for they have no such thing."
- **Aim for the two-sided response.** Patient in difficulty, active in obedience during ease — the profile Ibn Kathir draws out, and the one the hadith calls wonderful, because for such a person nothing Allah decrees is ever a loss.

passages.title: Give kin their due; usury versus charity
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a truth about provision and turn it into a way of living with money. Because Allah alone opens and closes the doors of sustenance, the believer is told where his wealth must go (ayah 38), what secretly corrupts giving (ayah 39), and why no one else deserves to be turned to at all (ayah 40). The thread holding them together is a single question: *whose hand is your provision really in, and who are you giving for?*

## Where the passage begins: the verse just before it

Ayah 38 opens with "So give…" — it is drawing a conclusion from what came immediately before it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that connection: in the preceding verse Allah stated that the provision of sustenance is His sole prerogative. He makes it abundant for whom He likes and curtails it whenever and for whomever He wills.

The practical message of that, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is unmistakable: **whoever spends in the way of Allah does not have his sustenance made to dwindle, and whoever acts miserly and tries to accumulate what he has does not find his possessions expand.** Once you truly believe that the supply line runs from Allah and not from your own grip, generosity stops feeling like loss.

So the address goes out — to the Prophet ﷺ and, as Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said, to every person privileged with abundance — not to be close-fisted with the wealth Allah has graced him with, but to spend it on the needy cheerfully.

## "Their due" — the word that changes everything

Ayah 38 names three recipients:

**1. Dhū al-qurbā — the close relative.** Ibn Kathīr explains this as "his due of respect and upholding the ties of kinship."

**2. Al-miskīn — the needy.** Ibn Kathīr defines him precisely: the one who has nothing to spend on his needs, *or* who has something but it is not enough. Poverty here is not only destitution; it includes the person whose income simply does not stretch far enough.

**3. Ibn al-sabīl — literally "the son of the road."** Ibn Kathīr: the traveller who is in need of money and other things during his journey. A man may be wealthy at home and stranded on the road; the Qurʼān sees him.

But the word that reframes the whole verse is **ḥaqqahu — "his due", "his right."** Allah does not say "give them something" or "be kind to them." He says give them *their right*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication with real force: this is a right that has been obligated upon your wealth, and therefore **no favour should be shown when giving it, because passing on someone's share to him is an act of fairness and justice, not a favour.**

That single choice of word dismantles the posture of the patron. The relative who receives from you is not in your debt. You are not the benefactor; you are the person settling an account.

## How wide is "kin"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that, as the majority of the commentators explained, *dhū al-qurbā* here apparently means common relatives — whether *maḥrams* (those relatives one may never marry) or otherwise. Likewise "his right" is stated in general terms and so encompasses:

- **obligatory rights** — such as those of parents, children and other close relations; and
- **voluntary acts of beneficence and charity** — which carry greater reward when done for close relations than when performed in favour of a non-relative.

So much so, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, that the Imām of tafsīr **Mujāhid** said that the charity of a person who neglects his own close relatives and gives it to someone else is not acceptable in the sight of Allah. Charity is not a way of escaping the people who have a claim on you.

## When you have nothing to give

Here the passage becomes unusually merciful, and unusually demanding.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: **the right of close relatives is not restricted to financial support.** It includes looking after them and providing any physical service to them. And if nothing else is within one's means, they may at least be treated sympathetically and consoled in their distress.

Sayyidnā Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the one who enjoys abundance in wealth should help his close relatives with money, and the one who does not have it should provide physical service and console them verbally (cited from Qurṭubī). The same principle, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, applies to the indigent and the traveller after the relatives: monetary help if you have the means, and otherwise physical service and consolation may discharge the right.

This closes the most common escape route. "I have nothing" is not an exemption from the verse — it only changes the currency in which the right is paid. Presence, errands, time, a visit, a word that steadies someone in their distress: these are payment.

## "Those who seek Allah's Face"

Ayah 38 closes: *That is best for those who seek Allah's Face; and it is they who will be successful.*

Ibn Kathīr explains "seeking Allah's Face" as meaning **to look upon Him on the Day of Resurrection, which is the ultimate aim.** Understand what that does to the verse: the giving is not transacted for a return in this world at all. The reward being sought is a *face turned toward Allah*, and, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, the ultimate aim of looking upon Him on that Day.

And "they who will be successful" — *al-mufliḥūn* — means successful, says Ibn Kathīr, **in this world and the Hereafter.** Not compensated later for a loss now. Successful in both.

## Ayah 39: two kinds of giving, told apart by intention

Now the passage puts two givers side by side. Both hand over wealth. Everything separates them.

*And that which you give in ribā, in order that it may increase from other people's property, has no increase with Allah; but that which you give in zakāh seeking Allah's Face — then those, they shall have manifold increase.*

**What is meant by ribā here?** Ibn Kathīr reports the interpretation: **that which is given as a gift to others in the hope that they will give back more than they were given.** There is no reward for this with Allah. He names those who understood the ayah this way: **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, Muḥammad bin Kaʿb and ash-Shaʿbī.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the custom this is correcting, and it is startlingly familiar: when people extend a gift or present to relatives — especially at the time of marriages — they make a note of the amount they have given, in the hope of getting back an equal amount when their turn comes, rather a little more. In Urdu the custom is known as *neota*. The verse emphasises that the rights of relatives commanded in the preceding ayah be discharged in a way that **neither shows it as a favour, nor gives it in the hope of any return.**

**Why call that "ribā"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles the scholarly discussion carefully, so it is worth reporting as a genuine difference of view rather than a settled matter:

- *Ribā* is a term commonly understood as equivalent to usury or interest, whose prohibition is detailed in Sūrah al-Baqarah 275–281 and Sūrah Āl ʿImrān 130. Since, according to a large number of scholars, usury was prohibited in Madinah while this ayah is Makkan, the word here cannot mean usury or interest — hence the interpretation as a gift given to a relative in order to get back a gift of higher value.
- **Some other commentators** take *ribā* here in the same sense as in al-Baqarah, i.e. usury and interest, arguing that usury was prohibited even in Makkah, and that only its implementation at state level was carried out in Madinah.

Mufti Muḥammad Taqī ʿUsmānī notes that the esteemed author reconciled the two views: the direct purpose of the verse is to correct the evil custom of giving gifts in the hope of getting a higher return — as mentioned in some traditions — while **the word *ribā* is used to indicate that this practice is tantamount to the practice of usury**, where an increased amount is charged from a debtor.

That is the sting of the word. A gift given to harvest a larger gift is not generosity wearing a smaller hat; the Qurʼān files it alongside lending at interest. In both, wealth leaves your hand only as bait.

## The wordplay you can hear in Arabic

The verse turns on one root, **r-b-w**, which carries the sense of *growing, increasing* — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders *ribā* here as "increased amount":

- **ribā** — the "increase" you engineer,
- **li-yarbuwa** — "so that it may increase" in the wealth of the people,
- **fa-lā yarbū ʿinda-llāh** — "it does not increase **with Allah**."

The wealth may genuinely grow in the ledger. The verse does not deny that. It denies growth *ʿinda-llāh* — in the only place growth is finally counted. And then the contrast: those who give zakāh seeking Allah's Face are **al-muḍʿifūn**, the ones who shall have manifold increase. Ibn Kathīr: those are the ones for whom **Allah will multiply the reward.**

Two people give away money. One arranges his own increase and receives nothing that lasts. The other seeks nothing, and Allah takes over the multiplying.

## From the Sunnah: the date that becomes a mountain

Ibn Kathīr cites here a report **in the Ṣaḥīḥ** (he does not name the collection further):

> No person gives in charity the equivalent of a date which was earned in a lawful manner, but the Most Merciful takes it in His Right Hand and takes care of it for its owner, just as any one of you takes care of his foal or young camel, until the date becomes the size of Mount Uḥud.

Several things are worth sitting with.

**"Earned in a lawful manner."** The multiplication begins at the source. Only what was lawfully acquired is taken up in this way.

**"Takes it in His Right Hand… and takes care of it for its owner."** The wording is conveyed exactly as the report gives it. Notice what it says about where your charity goes: it does not simply pass to the poor and end there. The Most Merciful takes it, and He takes care of it for the one who gave it.

**"Just as one of you takes care of his foal or young camel."** Notice the image chosen. It is not a coin dropped into a vault; it is a living thing being *reared*. The Arabic verb — *yurabbīhā*, from that same root **r-b-w** that gave us *ribā* — is the very word for the growth the usurer chased. The ayah says your engineered increase does not grow with Allah; the report says the charity you let go of is grown *by* Allah. The root is the same; the hand doing the growing is not.

And the arithmetic is deliberately overwhelming — a single date, honestly earned, ends up the size of Mount Uḥud. That is the scale of the "manifold increase" ayah 39 promised.

## A ruling on gifts

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a practical ruling with two sides, and both sides matter:

- **For the giver:** it is extremely contemptible to extend a gift to someone while expecting a return for it; this is what the verse forbids.
- **For the receiver:** it is morally desirable to try to give a gift back to that person of his own accord, whenever he finds a suitable occasion. This was exactly the practice of the Prophet ﷺ — he used to give a present to the person who gave him one (Qurṭubī, on the authority of Sayyidah ʿĀʼishah, may Allah be pleased with her). However, one should avoid giving him the impression that the gift is being given in return for his own.

Read the two together and you see the etiquette the passage is building: **expect nothing from anyone; give freely to everyone.** The duty to reciprocate lives in the heart of the one who received, never in the calculation of the one who gave.

## Ayah 40: why the passage ends in tawḥīd

*Allah is He Who created you, then provided food for you, then will cause you to die, then He will give you life. Is there any of your partners that does anything of that? Glory be to Him! And exalted be He above all that they associate.*

At first this looks like a change of subject. It is not — it is the foundation the whole passage has been standing on. The preceding verse said provision is Allah's prerogative; ayah 38 told you to release it; ayah 39 warned you not to secretly bill someone for it. Ayah 40 now tells you exactly who you are dealing with.

Ibn Kathīr traces the four acts:

- **"Created you, then provided food for you"** — He is the Creator and Provider. He brings man forth from his mother's womb naked and knowing nothing, not able to see or hear, and having no strength. Then He provides him with all these things — household effects, clothing, wealth, possessions and earnings.
- **"Then will cause you to die"** — after this life.
- **"Then He will give you life"** — on the Day of Resurrection.

Then the challenge: **"Is there any of your partners"** — Ibn Kathīr: those whom you worship instead of Allah — **"that does anything of that?"** None of them are able to do any of it. Allah is the One Who is Independent in His powers of creation, provision, and giving life and death, and then He will resurrect His creation on the Day of Resurrection.

Which is why the ayah closes as it does. Ibn Kathīr on *Glory be to Him! And exalted be He above all that they associate*: exalted, sanctified and glorified be He far above having any partner, peer, equal, son or father — for He is the One, the Unique, the Self-Sufficient Master, Who begets not nor was He begotten, and there is none comparable unto Him.

Look at the sequence once more and notice the mercy in it. The One asking you to open your hand is the One who provided for you when you arrived in this world naked, knowing nothing, unable even to ask. The provision was never yours to originate; it was placed in your hands mid-stream. And it will not be your last dealing with Him either — death and resurrection are on the same list, in the same hand.

## Living it

The passage asks for a few concrete things, and no more than it asks for:

**Treat family claims as claims, not charity.** Before you look for a cause, look at the relatives who have a right upon your wealth. Mujāhid's warning is severe: the charity of one who neglects his own close relatives and gives it to someone else is not acceptable in the sight of Allah.

**Give without the posture of the benefactor.** You are passing on someone's share — an act of fairness and justice, not a favour. That rules out the reminder, the leverage, the story told later.

**Give without the invoice.** No mental ledger of who owes you a return, and no gift issued at a wedding or an occasion as a deposit toward one — this is exactly the *neota* habit ayah 39 corrects, and the Qurʼān chose the word *ribā* for it.

**If you have no money, pay in the other currency.** Physical service, looking after them, and consoling them in their distress. Sayyidnā Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him) treated that as the discharge of the very same duty by the one who lacks means.

**Repay gifts you receive, quietly.** Follow the Prophet's ﷺ practice of giving a present to the one who gave him — while taking care not to give the impression that it is being given in return.

**Check the source before you count the reward.** Only what was earned in a lawful manner is taken up and cared for like a young camel.

**And keep the aim clean.** *Seeking Allah's Face* — which Ibn Kathīr says means to look upon Him on the Day of Resurrection, the ultimate aim — is the one intention this passage will accept, and the one that turns a date into a mountain.

passages.title: Corruption on land and sea; stand firm
passages.tafsir:
This passage draws a line between how people live and what the world becomes. Ayah 41 announces that the visible ruin of land and sea traces back to human hands; ayah 42 sends the listener out to walk among the ruins of earlier nations; and ayat 43–45 turn from diagnosis to remedy — set your face to the upright religion now, before a Day arrives that nobody can push back, when humanity splits in two and each person meets what he prepared.

What holds the five together is a single logic: **deeds have consequences, the consequences are being shown to you in small doses now, and the whole point of the small dose is to make you turn before the full reckoning.**

## "Corruption has appeared" — what exactly appeared?

Ibn Kathir preserves several readings of *al-barr* and *al-bahr* in ayah 41, each opening a different window.

- **Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and others**: *al-barr* means the empty land or wilderness, and *al-bahr* means towns and cities. A report from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah specifies that *al-bahr* refers to towns and cities built on the banks of rivers.
- **Others** took the words in their ordinary sense: land and sea.
- **Zayd bin Rafi'** read the corruption as withheld rain: "The rain is withheld from the land and this is followed by famine, and it is withheld from the sea, adversely affecting the animals which live in it."
- **Mujahid**, in a report Ibn Abi Hatim recorded: "Evil on land means the killing of the son of Adam, and evil on the sea means piracy."

The ayah covers the countryside and the city, the crop and the fish, the murder and the robbery. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting the author of *Ruh ul-Maʿani*, widens it further still: *fasad* here means **all sorts of calamities — famine, epidemic disease, frequent fires, drownings, the draining of Allah's blessing out of everything, and shrinking profits and mounting losses in businesses that ought to be profitable.**

We call famine a disaster and a bad quarter a market condition; this ayah puts both on one list.

## "Because of what the hands of people have earned"

The cause is named as *earning* — something people worked for and acquired, not something that fell on them from nowhere. Taking the first opinion above, Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that **the shortfall in crops and fruits is because of sins.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion — that the cause of calamities falling in the world is the sins and evil acts people commit — and then ranks those causes: **shirk (associating partners with Allah) and disbelief are the most severe of them all, and other sins follow after them.**

Abu Al-'Aliyah puts the principle in one sentence: *"Whoever disobeys Allah in the earth has corrupted it, because the good condition of the earth and the heavens depends on obedience to Allah."*

Ibn Kathir supports it with the hadith recorded by **Abu Dawud**: *"Any prescribed punishment which is carried out in the land is better for its people than if it were to rain for forty days."* His reasoning: when the prescribed punishments are actually carried out, most or many people are deterred from violating Allah's prohibitions; and when people give up sin, that becomes a cause of blessing in the skies and on the earth. **The more justice is established, the more the blessings and good things increase.**

Ibn Kathir illustrates from both ends of history. Looking forward: when 'Isa bin Maryam, peace be upon him, descends at the end of time and judges by this Shariʿah — killing the pigs, breaking the cross, abolishing the Jizyah, accepting nothing but Islam or the sword; and when Allah destroys the Dajjal and his followers, and Ya'juj and Ma'juj in his time, the earth will be told to bring forth its blessing, so that groups of people will eat from a single pomegranate and shelter in the shade of its skin, and the milk of one pregnant camel will suffice a whole group. All of this, Ibn Kathir says, from the blessings that follow the application of the Shariʿah of Muhammad ﷺ.

Looking backward, he cites what Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal recorded from Abu Qahdham: in the time of Ziyad or Ibn Ziyad, a man found a cloth wrapped around grains of wheat as big as date stones, and written on it: *"This grew at a time when justice prevailed."*

And it was reported in the Sahih that **when the evildoer dies, it is a relief for the people, the land, the trees and the animals.** A single person's wrongdoing is not a private matter; the soil feels it.

Some scholars concluded that when a man commits an evil deed he harms all humankind — and the beasts, the birds and the animals too — because the calamity his sin invites falls on everyone; so on the Day of Judgement every one of those sufferers will lodge a claim against him. **Shaqiq Zahid** said that whoever acquires something unlawfully harms not only the person he took it from but the whole of humanity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds two reasons of its own: such an act opens the door for others to follow, so that the whole of humanity gets drawn into the practice; and the evil practice invites the calamities that then bring trouble on everyone.

## The mercy hidden in the wording: "a part"

Ayah 41 does not say *that He may make them taste what they have done.* It says **"that He may make them taste a part of what they have done."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this alongside the parallel ayah, *"Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned — and He pardons much"* (42:30), and draws out the arithmetic of divine mercy: many sins are pardoned outright, many are punished only slightly, others are left unpunished altogether, and **only a few are ever answered with calamity. If every sin were punished with the intensity it deserves, nobody would be left alive in the world.**

Then comes the closing word of the ayah: **"so that they may return."** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply — return *from disobedience* — and compares it with *"And We tried them with good and evil in order that they might turn"* (7:168). Ibn Kathir also explains *"that He may make them taste a part"* as meaning that Allah tries people with the loss of wealth, of souls, and of fruits — **as a test and as a punishment for what they have done.**

Yet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion that makes this passage bearable: whatever trouble is sent down in this world, **though it comes as a result of misdeeds, is in reality a blessing and a grace from Allah, if only one would ponder.** The purpose of the pain is to wake people from their slumber so that they abandon the evil they are doing — which naturally works out in their own favour and brings them blessings.

## Ayah 42: go and look at the ruins

*"Say: Travel in the land and see what was the end of those before you."* Ibn Kathir explains "those before" as simply the people who came before you, and *"most of them were idolaters"* as an instruction to **see what happened to them when they rejected the Messengers and were ungrateful for blessings.**

This is an argument you make with your feet. And the diagnosis the ayah supplies is specific: what marked those ruined nations was *shirk* — associating partners with Allah — together with rejecting the Messengers and being ungrateful for what they had been given.

## The hard question: then why do the righteous suffer?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection honestly, and its answer is the most valuable thing in this passage for anyone living through hardship.

The objection begins from what is recorded in authentic ahadith — that the Prophet ﷺ said **this world is a prison for the believers and a heaven for the disbelievers.** (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the saying without naming a collection.) The commentary then supplies its own elaboration: that disbelievers receive the return for their good deeds in this world only, in the form of wealth and health, while the believer's reward is stored up to be given in the Hereafter; and that the believer in this world is like the branch of a tree, drifting from side to side in the breeze and standing still only when the breeze stops, and he leaves the world in that very condition. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates — again without naming a collection — that **worldly tribulations afflict the prophets most severely, then those nearest to them, then those nearest to them.** And plain experience seems to agree: believers often live hard lives while the impious live comfortably. If suffering tracked sin, surely it would be the other way round.

**The answer**, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, is that ayah 41 names sin as *a* cause of calamity, not as the *sole and complete* cause (*ʿillat tāmmah*) — that is, not a cause such that whenever anyone is afflicted, it must be because of his sins. As a rule, when a cause is present its effect normally follows; but in certain cases another cause overtakes it, suppressing or altogether cancelling the normal effect. Purgatives are used to move the bowels, but sometimes they do not, because of another drug or some unknown reason; likewise fever-reducers sometimes fail to bring a fever down. So: **it is one of the traits of sin to invite trouble, but a competing factor may prevent the trouble from arriving — and trouble may also arrive where there was no sin at all, since the ayah nowhere rules that out.** In the case of prophets and pious persons, calamity may visit them without sin: there the cause is not sin but the raising of their rank through tests and trials.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Qur'an assigns **sin** as the reason for calamities of the kind that **engulf the whole world or an entire city**, striking humans and animals alike — and such calamities normally fall when sins are committed openly and freely. **The rule does not transfer to individual hardship.** An individual's affliction may be a test, and when he passes it his position is raised in the Hereafter; in truth such calamities prove to be blessings and graces from Allah.

From this follow two conclusions the commentary states outright:

- **It is not correct to call someone a sinner because a calamity has struck him.**
- **It is not correct to consider someone pious and righteous because he is affluent.**

At the same time, the general principle stands: the main reason for great public afflictions — famine, storms, epidemics, inflation, the lack of Allah's blessing — is **sin committed openly and in defiance of Allah's rule.**

## Shah Waliyyullah: two layers of causation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note from Shah Waliyyullah in *Hujjat Allah al-Balighah*.

He says every good or evil, every trouble or comfort, every difficulty or ease in this world has **two kinds of causes: outward and inward.** Outward causes are the material ones everybody sees and acknowledges. Inward causes are those based on human actions, which draw either the help of the angels or their aversion.

His example is rain. To the scientists and philosophers, rain is vapour forming into cloud over the oceans through heat, drifting inland on the breeze, freezing in the cooler upper air, then thawing in the sun's heat and falling as drops. But the ahadith on the subject tell us this whole process is an act of the angels. **There is no contradiction: one process can have many causes.** The scientific account is the outward cause; the action of the angels is the inward one. When both combine, the rain falls as needed; when they do not, the rainfall may be interrupted.

He then notes that some causes of worldly hardship are simply physical or biological and recognise neither good nor bad. **It is the characteristic of fire to burn**, whether the person is pious or a sinner — unless it receives a divine command to act otherwise, as when the fire of Namrud was commanded to cool down and be tranquil for Sayyidna Ibrahim, peace be upon him. It is the attribute of water to drown heavy bodies, and it will always act to perform that duty.

Human deeds work as a second layer alongside these. When outward and inward causes of ease and comfort join together, a person or a group lives in ease. When the natural causes bring distress **and** the person's actions also call for trouble, calamity falls as a rule. But when the material causes push toward disaster while a person's good deeds incline toward ease, **the inward causes are consumed in countering the outward ones**, so he does not reap their full benefit. And when the material causes favour comfort while his actions invite trouble, neither full comfort nor the full toll of calamity arrives.

Understand this properly, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, and the apparent clash between the ayah and those ahadith disappears.

## Is this affliction a test or a punishment?

When calamities fall, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, they come to some good people as a trial and test — to atone for their sins or raise their status — and to others as punishment for their sins. From the outside the two look alike. The commentary offers two ways to tell them apart from the inside — and both are about **your response**, not about the event.

**Shah Waliyyullah's sign:** the calamity that comes as a test is recognised by **endurance with contentment**, which is itself a gift from Allah. Such people remain happy and contented in trouble, like a patient who accepts bitter medicine or painful surgery — he does not merely refrain from complaining about the pain, he pays the fees and deploys every resource he has to be treated in that painful way. The evildoers, on whom calamity falls as punishment, take it to heart, cry and moan against what they are suffering, and sometimes utter words of ingratitude to the extent of blasphemy.

**Ashraf Thanavi's sign:** if hardship makes you **aware of your own sins and faults and more inclined to seek Allah's pardon**, that is a sign of His kindness and favour. If it leaves you frustrated and indulging further in sin and evil, that is a sign of His wrath.

Both scholars close with *"and Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best"* — the honest posture for anyone reading another's suffering, or his own.

## Ayat 43–45: stand firm, and hurry

The passage now gives the only sane response. Ibn Kathir summarises ayat 43–45 in one line: **here Allah commands His servants to hasten to obedience to Him and to hasten to do good deeds.**

**"So set your face to the straight and right religion"** (ayah 43) — the image is of turning your whole face in one direction and holding it there, undivided. And the deadline is set: **"before there comes from Allah a Day which none can avert."** Ibn Kathir identifies it as the Day of Resurrection: when Allah wants it to happen, no one will be able to avert it. The urgency here is not manufactured; the door closes on a schedule you do not control.

**"On that Day men shall be divided"** (end of ayah 43). Ibn Kathir explains: they will be separated — **one group in Paradise and another in Hell.** Whatever mixing and blending of people the world allows, that Day sorts them cleanly, once.

Ayah 44 then states each side's account. **"Whosoever disbelieves will suffer from his disbelief"** — he alone carries it. **"And whosoever does righteous good deeds, then such will prepare a good place for themselves"** — the good you do now is not a fee you pay to Allah; it is bedding you are laying out in advance for your own arrival.

And then ayah 45 reveals what the whole thing was really for: **"that He may reward those who believe and do righteous good deeds, out of His bounty."** Ibn Kathir underlines the phrase **"out of His bounty"** — He rewards them from His bounty, so that in return for one good deed a person receives the reward of ten, up to seven hundred like it, as much as Allah wills. Notice the asymmetry: the sinner is made to taste only **a part** of what he did (ayah 41), while the believer is repaid **many times over** what he did (ayah 45).

The passage's last clause is the sober counterweight: **"Verily, He likes not the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir adds the necessary balance — *yet He is still just with them and does not oppress them.* It licenses no thought that they are treated unfairly: Allah's bounty is beyond what is deserved, and His justice is never less than exact.

## What the passage asks of you

- **Read the world honestly.** When blessing drains out of a place — crops, safety, trade, health — ayah 41 tells you to look at what hands have been earning, starting with your own.
- **Treat your private sins as public acts.** On the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, a wrong you commit alone can draw a harm that lands on people, animals and trees who never chose it — and they will have a claim on the Day of Judgement.
- **Read your own hardship generously and other people's charitably.** Do not call the afflicted a sinner and do not call the affluent righteous. Instead run Ashraf Thanavi's test on yourself: is this pain driving me toward seeking Allah's pardon, or into frustration and more sin?
- **Take the small blow as an invitation.** "A part of what they did… so that they may return." Every difficulty short of ruin is a door left open.
- **Then move.** Set your face to the straight and right religion, and hurry — the Day comes on Allah's schedule, and it divides.

passages.title: Winds of mercy and the earth brought back to life
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take one ordinary thing — wind — and read it as a message. Wind is sent as a herald of rain; rain revives a dead land; and Ibn Kathir titles his comment on this section *"The Revival of the Earth is a Sign of the Resurrection."* Set inside that argument, almost as an aside, is a word of comfort to the Prophet ﷺ about messengers who were rejected before him.

## Ayah 46: four gifts riding on a single breeze

Ibn Kathir heads this ayah *"Among the Signs of Allah are the Winds,"* and treats it as a listing of the favours Allah does for His creatures. He explains the winds as **harbingers of His mercy** — meaning, he says plainly, that rain will follow them. Then the ayah unfolds what the wind is for:

- **"giving you a taste of His mercy"** — Ibn Kathir: this is "the rain which will come down and revive people and the land." The word chosen is *taste*: not the whole of His mercy, only a sip of it given here.
- **"that the ships may sail at His command"** — on the sea, Ibn Kathir says, "for they are driven by the wind."
- **"that you may seek of His bounty"** — this is commerce: "by trading, earning a living and travelling from one country to another, one region to another." The same moving air that waters the fields also carries the merchant's cargo.
- **"in order that you may be thankful"** — that you give thanks to Allah, Ibn Kathir writes, "for the innumerable favours He has done for you, both visible and hidden."

Water for the land, transport for the ships, livelihood for the traders — and the ayah ends on the response Allah asks for: not analysis, but gratitude. Note too "as He wills" and "on whom of His servants as He wills" in ayah 48: the wind is not a machine running on its own. It is under command.

## Ayah 47: a word of consolation dropped into the middle

Then the subject changes to Messengers. Ibn Kathir reads this as directly personal: **"These are words of consolation from Allah to His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ."** The message to him is that if many of his people and of mankind disbelieve in him, the Messengers before him were rejected too, despite the clear signs they brought — and Allah punished those who rejected and opposed them, and saved those who believed in them.

So the ayah has two halves that must be read together: `fantaqamnā` (We took vengeance) on those who committed crimes, and the rescue of the believers.

**"and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers."** This is one of the most striking statements in the Qur'an, because Allah binds Himself. Nothing outside Him can impose an obligation on Him; Ibn Kathir explains that this is **"a duty which Allah took upon Himself as a blessing and a favour to them,"** and he links it to another ayah where Allah says the same kind of thing: *"your Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself"* (6:54). The obligation is self-imposed, and its source is generosity, not constraint. When a promise is guaranteed by the One who cannot fail, it is more certain than anything a creature could enforce.

### A hadith that reads this phrase into daily life

Ibn Kathir cites a narration recorded by **Ibn Abi Hatim** from **Abu Ad-Darda'**, may Allah be pleased with him, who said he heard Allah's Messenger ﷺ say: *"No Muslim man defends the honour of his brother except that there would be a right upon Allah to defend him from the fire of Hell on the Day of Resurrection."* And then the Prophet ﷺ recited this very ayah — *and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers.*

Sit with how that reading works. The ayah's grand promise of divine backing is applied by the Prophet ﷺ to something small and unglamorous: defending a fellow Muslim's honour. Do that, and Allah takes upon Himself to defend you on the Day when you can defend yourself least of all. You help a believer; Allah's help of believers comes back to you.

### If Allah's help is guaranteed, why are Muslims ever defeated?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises exactly this objection. On the face of the words, one would expect that Muslims could never be defeated by disbelievers — yet on many occasions the result has been the opposite. Its answer works through several steps:

- The promise attaches to **"the believers"** in a specific sense: those who fight the disbelievers **purely for the sake of Allah**. It is such people whom Allah avenges and helps to overpower their adversaries.
- Where the outcome is different, it is **"due to some sort of slip on the part of the believers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the Qur'an's own account of the battle of Uhud: *"Shaitan had but made them slip for some of their deeds"* (3:155).
- Even then the promise is not withdrawn. Once they realise their fault, Allah graces them with victory and the upper hand — "as it happened in the battle of Uhud."
- Those who are "Muslims only by name," habitually defiant and negligent of the teachings of Islam, and not even penitent when the disbelievers gain the upper hand, are not included in this promise and do not qualify for that help.
- And yet the door is not closed: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends by noting that **Allah provides help by His grace on many occasions without anyone deserving it**, so it is always beneficial to beg for His mercy and to hope for His help.

That balance is worth holding onto. The promise is real and it is precise; it is not a licence for complacency, and its failure to appear is a summons to self-examination rather than to doubt about Allah.

## Ayah 48: watching a cloud being built

Now the passage returns to the wind and slows right down, and Ibn Kathir says the purpose here is that **Allah explains how He creates the clouds that rain the water.** Read the ayah as a sequence of camera shots:

**"He sends the winds, so that they raise clouds."** From where? Ibn Kathir reports it is "either from the sea, as was mentioned by more than one of the scholars, or from whatever Allah wills."

**"and spread them along the sky as He wills."** Ibn Kathir: "He spreads them and causes them to increase and grow. **From a little He makes a lot**, and creates the clouds that look like shields. Then He spreads them out until they fill the horizon." Sometimes, he adds, the clouds come from the sea already heavy and full, as in *"And it is He Who sends the winds as heralds of glad tidings, going before His mercy. Till when they have carried a heavy-laden cloud, We drive it to a land that is dead"* — an ayah which ends: *"Similarly, We shall raise up the dead, so that you may remember or take heed"* (7:57). That cross-reference matters: the same image elsewhere in the Qur'an ends in exactly the same conclusion this passage is heading toward.

**"and then break them into fragments"** — Arabic `kisafan`. Here the early authorities differed, and Ibn Kathir reports the disagreement rather than settling it:
- **Mujahid, Abu 'Amr bin Al-'Ala', Matar Al-Warraq and Qatadah**: it means *pieces*.
- **Ad-Dahhak** and others: it means *piled up*.
- Others still: it means *black*, because the clouds contained so much water — and sometimes they are heavy and close to the earth.

Anyone who has watched a sky before a downpour will recognise all three descriptions at once: torn into masses, stacked up, darkened with water.

**"until you see rain drops come forth from their midst"** — `al-wadq`, which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as the drops, the rain, which come from the midst of those clouds. The ayah puts *you* in it: **you see** it happen. This is not information to be accepted on authority; it is an invitation to look up.

**"Then when He has made them fall on whom of His servants as He wills, lo, they rejoice!"** Ibn Kathir: "They rejoice at the rain when it comes to them because of their need for it." The joy is measured by the need.

## Ayah 49: the despair just before the rain

`Lamublisīn` — they were in despair. Ibn Kathir fills in the human scene behind the word. These people "were in despair, thinking that rain would never fall, just before it came to them." They had been in need of it; there had been no rainfall for a long time; they were waiting for it at the time when it was due, but it did not come to them then. **The rain was late, and a long time passed.** Then the rain came to them suddenly, after they began to despair — and because it arrived at the time of greatest need, "it was a tremendous event for them." Their land had become dry and barren; then it "was stirred to life, and it swelled and produced every lovely kind of growth."

Ibn Kathir dwells on the waiting, and it is worth dwelling on. The delay is not a gap in the story; on his reading it is what made the arrival so tremendous.

## Ayah 50: look, and then draw the conclusion

**"Look then at the effects of Allah's mercy"** — `āthār`, the traces or effects; and Ibn Kathir specifies that the "mercy" here means **the rain**. The command is `fanẓur`: *look*. Not "consider the argument," but go and see the green coming up out of ground that was dead a month ago.

**"how He revives the earth after its death."** By this, Ibn Kathir writes, **"Allah draws attention to the revival of people's bodies after they have died and disintegrated into nothing."** That is the hinge of the whole passage. A revived earth is not merely a poetic comparison to resurrection; it is the working sample of it, laid out in front of everyone who has ever doubted.

**"Verily, that shall indeed raise the dead"** — Ibn Kathir: "the One Who does that is able to raise the dead." **"and He is able to do all things."** The argument is complete and it is short: you have watched Him do it to the earth; the objection to resurrection was never really about Allah's power.

## Living it

- **Let the weather preach.** Ayah 50 gives a command — *look* — and ayah 48 puts you in the scene: *you see* the drops emerge. Rain is meant to be watched with the question "who is doing this?" alive in you, not merely checked on a forecast.
- **Answer mercy with thanks.** Ayah 46 ends by naming the purpose of the whole chain: *that you may be thankful* — for the favours Ibn Kathir calls innumerable, "both visible and hidden."
- **Do not conclude from delay.** Ayah 49 describes people who had already given up when the rain arrived. Late is not never. Despair is the reading of someone who mistakes Allah's timing for Allah's absence.
- **Defend a fellow believer's honour** — the Prophet ﷺ, in the narration Ibn Kathir cites from Ibn Abi Hatim, made that the practical face of *Allah's help for the believers*.
- **Earn the promise.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of ayah 47 asks the believer to look first at their own slips when help seems withheld — and then, having done so, to keep asking, since Allah often gives help by His grace that no one had deserved.

And if you ever doubt that dust and bones can live again: Allah has already answered you, every spring, in a field.

passages.title: A withering wind, and hearts that cannot hear
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from the sky to the soul. Ayah 51 imagines a single dry wind that turns a ripening crop yellow, and shows how quickly people who had just been rejoicing over rain slide into denial. Ayat 52 and 53 then explain why: the problem was never the weather, it was hearts that have gone dead, deaf and blind — and no messenger, not even the Prophet ﷺ, can force such a heart to hear.

## The scene ayah 51 walks out of

Ayah 51 begins with "And if We send a wind," which means you have to know what wind came before it. In the immediately preceding ayat Allah describes Himself as the One who sends the winds so that they raise the clouds, spreads those clouds across the sky as He wills, breaks them into fragments, and brings the raindrops out from their midst — and when He makes that rain fall on whichever of His servants He wills, "lo, they rejoice."

Ibn Kathir notes that the joy in that scene is not casual joy. The rain was overdue: "there had been no rainfall for a long time, so they were waiting for it at the time when it was due, but it did not come." A long stretch passed and hope drained away. "Then the rain came to them suddenly, after they began to despair, and after their land became dry and barren, it was stirred to life, and it swelled and produced every lovely kind of growth." It arrived, he says, "at the time of greatest need, so it was a tremendous event for them."

Then comes the instruction: look at the traces of Allah's mercy, how He gives the earth life after its death. Ibn Kathir: "Thus Allah draws attention to the revival of people's bodies after they have died and disintegrated into nothing." The One who does this "is able to raise the dead." Hold on to that image of *life given back to what was dead*, because ayah 52 is about to turn the same image against the deniers.

## Ayah 51: one wind, and the whole memory is erased

**"And if We send a wind, and they see it turn yellow — behold, they then would become unthankful."**

Ibn Kathir explains the wind precisely: "a wind which dries up the crops which they have tended and cultivated and which have matured, and they see them turn yellow, and start to rot." This is not a storm that flattens a village. It is a hot, drying wind over a field that was almost ready — the labour of a whole season browning on the stalk.

And what does that produce? Ibn Kathir: "they would become ungrateful, i.e., they would deny the previous blessings that they were given." Read that carefully. The complaint is not only about the ruined crop. It reaches backwards and cancels the rain they had wept for. The blessing is not weighed at all; it is denied.

Ibn Kathir places beside this another passage of the Qur'an: "Then tell Me about the seed that you sow in the ground" — running through to the reaction of a people whose harvest is ruined, "Nay, but we are deprived!" (56:63–67). The wording of the complaint is instructive. Not *we have been tested*, not *He who gave can give again*, but a flat accusation of deprivation, as though the giving had never happened.

**This is the diagnosis of fair-weather faith.** Rain came after despair and produced rejoicing; one dry wind produces denial. If gratitude collapses that fast, it was never gratitude for the Giver — it was pleasure in the gift.

## Ayat 52–53: why the argument stops working

**"So verily, you cannot make the dead to hear, nor can you make the deaf to hear the call, when they show their backs and turn away. And you cannot guide the blind from their straying; you can make to hear only those who believe in Our Ayat, and have submitted."**

In Ibn Kathir's tafsir this passage carries the heading *The Disbelievers are like the Dead, Deaf and Blind*.
